text:
The Buffalo Bills’ players and coaches may have been on a bye week over the last several days, but that wasn’t the case for the majority of teams in the league in Week 7 as the NFL was jam packed with plenty of exciting action last weekend.

For Buffalo’s upcoming opponent—the Baltimore Ravens—things weren’t so exciting on Sunday, though, as the AFC North squad fell short at home to the Cincinnati Bengals, 35-13, after originally leading 13-0 at halftime. The loss marked the team’s second straight in its division to fall to 4-3 on the season under first-year head coach Jesse Minter.

Furthermore, Baltimore appears to have lost an important member of its offensive line during the last matchup with Cincinnati, as well, as NFL insiders Ian Rapoport and Mike Garafolo reported on Tuesday morning that Ravens’ starting offensive guard Olaivavega “Vega” Ioane, who was selected at pick No. 14 overall in the first round of the 2026 NFL Draft out Penn State this past spring, suffered a MCL sprain against the Bengals.

A 22-year-old native of Graham, Washington, Ioane was the fourth offensive lineman selected in the first round of April’s draft, but he was also the first guard to go off the board.

Seen by many talent evaluators as a sure-fire NFL starter, Ioane seamlessly transitioned into the starting lineup for Baltimore this offseason.

Making starts at right guard and center out of necessity due to various other injured players going down earlier this season up front for the Ravens, the former Nittany Lions’ lineman has been a solid presence along the offensive line during his first season as a professional.

In fact, according to the NFL’s Next Gen Stats, the 6-foot-4, 326-pound thumper allowed only a 4.6% pressure rate entering Week 6, and he surrendered zero sacks in 163 pass-blocking snaps (84 at RG, 79 at C), as well, making him the highest-rated rookie guard in the NFL in that critical department.

Baltimore’s list of ailments keep compounding entering Week 8

For that reason, the news of Ioane being sidelined for at least “a little bit” is certainly brutal information to receive at this juncture of the season, especially considering that Baltimore’s franchise veteran quarterback Lamar Jackson is likely set to return to the lineup after missing the past three games with an apparent ankle injury.

If the rookie stalwart is unable to suit up against the Bills this weekend at Highmark Stadium in Orchard Park, then it will mean that the Ravens will be trotting out their sixth different offensive line combination through the first eight weeks of 2026 campaign.

And, while that’s a sight that Buffalo’s AFC counterpart likely doesn’t want to see this weekend, it’s certainly a situation that the Bills and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard will have to capitalize on.

Bills’ interior DL needs to dominate with Ioane likely out

Whether it be up-and-coming defensive star Deone Walker or former top-10 pick Ed Oliver on the interior of Buffalo’s defensive front, someone on the defensive line needs to dominate their battle with Baltimore’s backup at right guard on Sunday.

The matchup between the Bills and Ravens has future playoff implications written all over it, so it’ll be imperative that Buffalo takes full advantage of any areas of weakness that their upcoming opponent might have.

The objective for first-year head coach Joe Brady has seemingly always been to reach the No. 1 seed in the AFC during his inaugural season as the head man in charge in Western New York, and that goal appears to be more in reach than ever before entering November 2026, especially after the Kansas City Chiefs just dropped their first game of the season on Sunday Night Football against the Seattle Seahawks.

Out of the bye week, Brady and Leonhard must create a plan of attack to push forward with vengeance over the final 11 games of the season.

Exploiting Baltimore’s shortcomings up front would be a great place to start on Sunday.

text:
concussionandcte

Verified

40m

A new study estimates 75% of former NFL players who died between 2008-2023 had CTE.

It’s a difficult number to confront, especially for former players and families already concerned about their brain health. But it’s also an important step forward in understanding CTE.

For years, researchers have found CTE in a high percentage of former NFL players whose brains were donated to science. But what about the players whose brains weren’t donated? This new study helps answer that question by accounting for potential bias in brain donations, providing a more representative estimate of CTE among deceased former NFL players.

As former NFL quarterback @hasselbeck puts it, knowing what we’re up against gives us a better chance of winning. And there’s reason for hope.

Every new discovery brings us closer to understanding CTE, developing ways to diagnose it during life, and ultimately finding effective treatments. This research can also help inform efforts to make the game safer for future generations.

Importantly, these findings don’t tell us how many living NFL players have CTE, and not everyone with CTE pathology develops symptoms.

For former players and families concerned about their brain health, you are not alone, and help is available.

Visit ConcussionAndCTE.org/HelpLine for guidance and support. Former NFL players can also access resources through The Trust Powered by the @NFLPA, the NFLPA’s Professional Athletes Foundation, and the NFL Life Line (800-453-0078), which provides independent, confidential support 24/7.

The study was published today in JAMA Network Open and led by @bu_cte in collaboration with @massgeneralbrigham and the Concussion & CTE Foundation.

text:
The Kansas City Chiefs had an uphill battle against the Seattle Seahawks on Sunday Night Football.

The Chiefs entered Sunday's matchup without starting right tackle Jaylon Moore, who was sidelined by a concussion, and left tackle Josh Simmons, who remained out with a back injury. They were also missing injured receivers Rashee Rice and Tyquan Thornton.

That showed up in the final score, as they were dominated 20-3. However, in the fourth quarter, when the game was still conceivably within reach, a critical error from Xavier Worthy left Patrick Mahomes uncharacteristically frustrated.

Fans, though, weren't fully sure if his reaction was justified.

Fans Take Notice of Patrick Mahomes' Frustration With Xavier Worthy

Coming into the game, the Chiefs had a top-10 unit in PFN's Offense Impact Metric. But a lot of that had to do with the explosion from Kenneth Walker III, who leads the league in rushing yards by a sizeable margin.

The passing game left a lot to be desired, and that was before their two best receivers went down with injuries. Against the Seahawks, as Walker struggled and finished with just 36 rushing yards, the depleted receiving corps wasn't enough to sustain the Chiefs.

Things came to a head in the fourth quarter. In what was shaping up to be their best drive of the game, the Chiefs came up to the 45-yard line. On 1st-and-10, Mahomes threw a perfect ball for Worthy to catch and run.

However, Worthy failed to secure the pass, prompting a visibly frustrated reaction from Mahomes. Although Kansas City continued moving the ball afterward, the possession ultimately ended without points when Harrison Butker missed a 45-yard field goal.

Worthy finished with only three catches for 11 yards on six targets, underscoring Kansas City's inability to generate meaningful production from its available wide receivers.

"You don't often see Patrick Mahomes show frustration like this," Henry McKenna of Fox Sports was quick to notice. "But after Xavier Worthy's drop… the QB was upset."

"Cause he's seen this for 3 years," one fan argued for Mahomes. "He's sick of this [expletive]… And I don't blame him."

SET YOUR LINEUPS: PFN's Free Fantasy Start/Sit Optimizer

One fan jokingly claimed, "He was seeing ghosts of Toney and Moore there," while another fan explained, "Inconsistency is the running theme for Chiefs WRs in recent years. Yes, Mahomes' reaction is warranted. Worthy making catches last week, then dropping crucial ones is absurd."

For one fan, though, it was becoming a more common sight to see Mahomes upset. With the offensive unit not working as seamlessly as it has over the years, he believes they have lost the punch they once had.

"You see frustration from Mahomes plenty of the time, especially over the last few years as the offense has performed worse and worse,"the fan claimed. "Should've known that things would never stay the way they were with Kelce & Hill."

For one fan, though, one drop from Worthy couldn't take away from an all-around underwhelming night for Mahomes. Coming into the game at number 10 in PFN's Quarterback Impact Metric, he finished with just 165 yards and an interception.

"Mahomes was awful," one fan announced. "So, let's not blame Worthy for Mahomes not being able to handle the Hawks' defense."

It remains to be seen if this was a blip for the Chiefs, given the particularly strenuous circumstances in this game, or a canary in the coal mine for the problems plaguing this roster. Still at 5-1, they are at the top of the AFC West, but the margin for error is slim.

With the Denver Broncos hot on their heels, Week 8's game could have major implications. And with the wide receiving room looking like it needs a clear upgrade, this game may have been the most obvious indicator of their need for a difference-maker.

title: How NFL Injury Protection Works After a Player Is Released - Football Nation
description:
The ordinary Injury Protection Benefit applies to the season after the injury season.
Injury Protection focuses on a severe football injury and future physical inability.
NFL Football Operations explains that injury guarantees are negotiated contract protection, while Article 45 creates a separate collectively bargained benefit.
Related Football Nation guide: How NFL Termination Pay Protects Vested Veterans The Article 45 qualification test Article 45, Section 2 requires the player’s contract to have been terminated by his club.
Guaranteed Paragraph 5 Salary for the next two seasons offsets Injury Protection and Extended Injury Protection dollar for dollar.
text:
A player can be released while still unable to play and still have a path to compensation in a later season. That path is NFL Injury Protection. It is a collectively bargained benefit, not a promise that every injured player receives the rest of his contract.

Information cutoff: October 28, 2026 at 3:57 AM Central. The governing source is the 2020 NFL and NFLPA Collective Bargaining Agreement, which runs through the 2030 season. This guide explains Article 45 as written and is educational, not legal advice.

What Article 45 protects

Article 45 covers a severe football injury from an NFL game or practice when a club terminates the player’s contract and the player remains unable to play through the required examination process. The ordinary Injury Protection Benefit applies to the season after the injury season. Extended Injury Protection can apply to the second season after the injury.

This is different from Termination Pay. Termination Pay protects certain vested veterans after a release for performance or roster reasons. Injury Protection focuses on a severe football injury and future physical inability. It also differs from an injury guarantee written into an individual contract. NFL Football Operations explains that injury guarantees are negotiated contract protection, while Article 45 creates a separate collectively bargained benefit.

Related Football Nation guide: How NFL Termination Pay Protects Vested Veterans

The Article 45 qualification test

Article 45, Section 2 requires the player’s contract to have been terminated by his club. The player must then satisfy each required condition.

1. The season ending condition

Section 2(a) says the player must have been physically unable to participate in all or part of the club’s final game because of a severe football injury, as certified after an examination by the club physician. Club authorized surgery in the following offseason can also satisfy this part.

2. Required rehabilitation

Section 2(b) requires the player to complete the reasonable and customary rehabilitation required by the club. The club pays those rehabilitation costs even if it no longer employs him.

3. The benefit physical

Section 2(c) requires the player to fail the club examination for Injury Protection on or before August 1 in the next season. The exam must be identified in writing as the Injury Protection examination. The club cannot avoid liability by refusing a timely exam when the player cooperates.

4. The contract link

Section 2(d) addresses an expired contract. If the player signs with the prior club for the next season, eligibility can continue when every other condition is met. A contract with a new club does not create the benefit under that new contract.

The examination is injury specific. It is not a general judgment that the player can never play again. A player may be unable to perform his position at the required NFL level on the exam date and still recover later.

What the benefit pays in 2026

Article 45, Section 3 starts with 100 percent of the player’s Paragraph 5 Salary for the season after the injury. Paragraph 5 Salary is the contract’s base salary. For the 2026 League Year, the benefit is capped at $2.1 million.

Guaranteed Paragraph 5 Salary for the next two seasons offsets Injury Protection and Extended Injury Protection dollar for dollar. Payments arrive in equal weekly installments no later than the first regular season game, and they stop if the player signs with another club for that season. A player may receive the ordinary Injury Protection Benefit only once during his NFL career.

The salary cap treatment is split. Article 45, Section 4 assigns up to $1.26 million of a 2026 payment to the prior club’s Team Salary. The balance, up to the $2.1 million maximum, is a Player Benefit Cost.

Related Football Nation guide: How Void Years Work in NFL Contracts and the Salary Cap

Extended Injury Protection

Sections 7 and 8 create a second layer for the second season after the injury. The player generally must have qualified for the first benefit, must have a contract covering the second season, must remain unable to play because of the same severe football injury, must continue the required rehabilitation, and must fail the former club’s designated examination before June 1.

For 2026, Extended Injury Protection equals 100 percent of Paragraph 5 Salary for that second season, capped at $1.05 million unless the player negotiated greater protection. Guaranteed salary offsets it. The benefit is also limited to once in a career and stops if the player signs with another club for that season.

Article 45, Section 12 sets separate deadlines. An ordinary Injury Protection grievance must be initiated by October 15 of the League Year in which the benefit is claimed. A player seeking the extended benefit must notify the former club and the NFL in writing by January 31 that he believes he remains physically unable to play.

Two realistic examples

Example 1: base salary below the cap

A defensive tackle suffers a serious knee injury in December, misses the club’s final game, follows the club rehabilitation plan and fails the Injury Protection physical before August 1. The club terminates his contract. His next season Paragraph 5 Salary is $1.4 million and none is guaranteed. If the other Article 45 conditions are met, the benefit begins at $1.4 million because that salary is below the 2026 maximum.

Example 2: salary above the cap with an offset

A receiver has a $3 million Paragraph 5 Salary scheduled for the next season and $800,000 of that salary is guaranteed. He satisfies Section 2. The 2026 benefit is first limited to $2.1 million, then the $800,000 guaranteed salary offsets the benefit. The remaining Article 45 amount is $1.3 million. If the facts or contract language differ, the result can change.

Injury grievance, injury settlement and Injury Protection are not the same

The NFLPA describes an injury grievance as a claim that a player was released while unable to play. It generally seeks salary from the season of release and must usually be filed within 25 days. Article 45 protection concerns later seasons and uses its own deadlines. The NFLPA also warns that an injury settlement can end treatment obligations, current year salary claims and future Injury Protection rights. Released and settled should never be treated as interchangeable.

A roster transaction such as injured reserve answers a different question. Remaining under contract on injured reserve is not the same as being released and pursuing Article 45 benefits. Activation from the physically unable to perform list signals roster availability, not an Article 45 award.

Related Football Nation guide: What Does IR Mean in Fantasy Football?

Related Football Nation report: Lions Place Tom Kennedy, Ben Bartch and Devin White on Injured Reserve

Related Football Nation report: Steelers Activate Jalen Ramsey From PUP

Football and roster consequence

The rule gives clubs a financial reason to track severe injuries beyond the season in which they happen. A release does not automatically erase the prior club’s obligation. Medical certification, rehabilitation records, exam dates and the old contract all matter. For a front office, the question is not simply whether the player occupies a roster spot. It is whether Article 45 creates a future payment and cap charge.

Fantasy consequence

An Injury Protection claim is evidence of a serious recovery problem at a defined exam date, but it is not a return timetable and it does not predict a depth chart role. Fantasy managers should treat it as context that the player was not ready for football activity when examined. The next actionable checkpoints are a new contract, a passed physical, roster placement and practice participation. The benefit itself does not make the player more likely to produce fantasy points.

The strongest counterargument

The strongest criticism is that Injury Protection sounds broader than it is. That criticism is fair. The benefit is conditional, capped, offset by guaranteed salary, tied to strict medical and filing steps, and generally available only once in a career. It is not full contract insurance. Its value is narrower: it prevents a qualifying severe football injury from becoming a total financial cliff merely because the club terminated the contract.

Common misconceptions

Misconception: every player released while hurt gets the next year’s salary. Reality: Article 45 requires the severe football injury, rehabilitation, examination and contract conditions in Section 2.

Misconception: the benefit means the entire contract is guaranteed. Reality: the calculation uses Paragraph 5 Salary, applies a 2026 maximum and includes offsets.

Misconception: filing an injury grievance automatically secures Article 45 money. Reality: the grievance for the release season and the later season benefit are distinct claims with different rules and deadlines.

Misconception: a player receiving the benefit cannot return. Reality: payments stop if he signs with another club for that season. The rule protects recovery, not retirement.

Frequently asked questions

Does the club pay rehabilitation costs after release?

Yes, when the rehabilitation is the reasonable and customary treatment required under Article 45, Section 2(b). Section 13 also assigns reasonable rehabilitation and club requested examination travel costs to the club.

Can a player collect the benefit twice after two different injuries?

The ordinary benefit is limited to once during an NFL playing career. The extended benefit also has a once per career limit.

Does workers’ compensation disappear?

No. Article 45, Section 11 coordinates the benefits. It treats 50 percent of Injury Protection payments as equivalent to workers’ compensation indemnity and permits a corresponding offset against qualifying state indemnity awards, but not medical coverage awards.

What should readers watch next?

The next checkpoints are the August 1 ordinary benefit physical, the October 15 ordinary claim deadline, the January 31 extended notice deadline and the June 1 extended benefit physical. Individual players should rely on the NFLPA and qualified counsel for case specific advice.

Sources checked

NFL and NFLPA Collective Bargaining Agreement, Article 45, Sections 2 through 13. Checked October 28, 2026 at 3:57 AM Central.

NFLPA grievance explainer. Checked October 28, 2026 at 3:57 AM Central.

NFLPA injury settlement explainer. Checked October 28, 2026 at 3:57 AM Central.

title: 2028 NFL Draft Picture Uncertain as Projected No. 1 QB Suffers Season-Ending Injury
description:
Four games into the season, Kamario Taylor had 14 touchdown passes, an unbeaten Mississippi State team, and a place in the Heisman conversation.
His breakout also carried implications beyond the Bulldogs’ season, putting him among the quarterbacks to watch for the 2028 NFL Draft.
“Sources: Mississippi State star QB Kamario Taylor will miss the rest of the season, as he faces surgery on his injured toe.
His injury interrupted that early momentum just as Mississippi State entered the tougher stretch of its SEC schedule.
The Macon, Mississippi, native has expressed his commitment to staying at Mississippi State.
text:
Four games into the season, Kamario Taylor had 14 touchdown passes, an unbeaten Mississippi State team, and a place in the Heisman conversation. His breakout also carried implications beyond the Bulldogs’ season, putting him among the quarterbacks to watch for the 2028 NFL Draft. But sustaining that rise would prove more complicated than his fast start suggested.

“Sources: Mississippi State star QB Kamario Taylor will miss the rest of the season, as he faces surgery on his injured toe. Taylor has an appointment today to get his toe checked out by a specialist and could have surgery as early as tomorrow. He’s expected to make a full recovery,” ESPN’s Pete Thamel reported on X.

Taylor first injured his toe during Mississippi State’s win over Missouri on September 26. The school announced the decision on Tuesday. The goal is to help him recover in time for the 2027 season. Thamel shared more details in another post.

“Sources said that Taylor pushed hard to play after the injury. It became clear that time and rest weren’t going to get to him to a point where he could be effective.”

Taylor tried to play against Alabama on October 3 and Oklahoma on Saturday, but the injury clearly affected him. He left both games early and missed the Bulldogs’ October 17 game against LSU.

Against Oklahoma, Taylor appeared to hurt his toe further when he was tackled during a scramble. Mississippi State lost the game 23-15. However, head coach Jeff Lebby said Taylor had aggravated his existing injury and had not suffered a new one.

The injury comes at a difficult time for Taylor. Before it happened, he was one of college football’s breakout stars. He helped Mississippi State start the season 4-0, with wins over Minnesota, South Carolina, and Missouri. The Bulldogs also climbed into the national top 25.

That start also put Taylor in the Heisman Trophy conversation. Through four games, he was tied for the national lead with 14 touchdown passes and had climbed to third in BetMGM’s Heisman odds. His injury interrupted that early momentum just as Mississippi State entered the tougher stretch of its SEC schedule.

His performance against then-No. 19 Missouri was a highlight. Taylor completed 27 of 38 passes for 360 yards, three touchdowns, and one interception.

Taylor finished his season with 1,460 passing yards and 17 touchdown passes. He completed more than 65% of his passes before the injury cut his season short.

He also contributed on the ground, finishing with 147 rushing yards and one touchdown on 46 carries. That brought his combined passing and rushing production to 1,607 yards and 18 touchdowns.

At 6-foot-4 and 230 pounds, Taylor is already attracting attention as a future NFL prospect. He currently ranks No. 1 on the consensus big board for the 2028 NFL Draft.

Taylor belongs to the 2025 recruiting class, meaning the 2027 season would be his third year in college. The 2028 NFL Draft would follow that season.

For now, the focus is on his recovery. Surgery is expected to help him get ready for the 2027 season, and Thamel reported that Taylor is expected to make a full recovery. However, it remains to be seen how missing the rest of this season will affect his future draft evaluation.

Mississippi State, meanwhile, has struggled since its strong start. The Bulldogs are 4-3 overall and 2-3 in SEC play after losing three straight games to Alabama, LSU, and Oklahoma. No. 11 Texas is next on their schedule.

With Taylor out for the season, Lebby must choose a starting quarterback. He has not named a replacement, but the decision rests between Billy Puckett, who has already filled in for Taylor this season, and Appalachian State transfer AJ Swann.

As the Bulldogs prepare to move forward without him, Taylor will focus on surgery and recovery ahead of the 2027 season. His procedure could take place as early as Wednesday. The Macon, Mississippi, native has expressed his commitment to staying at Mississippi State.

text:
Green Bay Packers superstar Micah Parsons is getting closer to his long-awaited return from last season's torn ACL.

Head coach Matt LaFleur told reporters on Monday he's hoping the dynamic edge-rusher returns to practice next week:

Parsons, 27, was traded by the Dallas Cowboys to the Packers ahead of the 2025 season and was having a fantastic debut season, registering 41 tackles (12 for loss), 12.5 sacks, 27 quarterback hits, two forced fumbles and a pass defensed in 14 games.

But he tore his ACL during a December matchup against the Denver Broncos, ending his season and calling into question when he would be able to return for the 2026 campaign.

The Packers could use him back. The team is tied for 15th in the NFL with 16 sacks on the season, though the pass defense has been solid in general (208 YPG, ninth in the NFL). Still, the team finds itself last in the loaded NFC North despite being 4-3 overall and has gone just 1-2 against its divisional rivals thus far.

Next week would make for a logical potential return point, at least to practice. Because the Packers play on Thursday night this week against the Carolina Panthers, they'll have a longer runway before a Week 9 contest against the New England Patriots. But the team also has a Week 11 bye, which means Parsons' return to game action might be delayed until Week 12.

"At the end of the day, that's the medical," LaFleur told reporters about how it will be decided to clear Parsons for practice. "I'm itching at it though, for sure."

text:
Rookie running back Jonah Coleman has played in only three games because of an ankle injury, and he might win the impact-per-snap-played quotient, but Waddle leads the Broncos in receptions (26) and receiving yards (276). His numbers would likely look better if he had not been caught up in the swirl of Denver’s passing struggles. Waddle left Sunday’s game because of an apparent shoulder injury, but if it’s not serious and the Broncos can simply get him the ball more, his output will improve along with their offense.

It’s unfair to just eliminate three long plays for a team and judge it on the rest of its production. Those explosive plays are earned. And the Broncos got a 62-yard touchdown run from Bo Nix, a 52-yard touchdown on a short pass to RJ Harvey and a 47-yard catch to Marvin Mims Jr. that set up a touchdown.

On the Broncos’ other 53 plays, they gained only 216 yards. That’s a middling 4 yards per play. Still, Sunday was another win. The Broncos are 5-2 and the Chiefs’ loss on Sunday sets up a game that should frame the rest of the AFC West race as the Chiefs visit Denver in Week 8. The Broncos will have to find some consistency on offense and they have a few key injuries to track: receiver Jaylen Waddle has a chest injury, defensive lineman Zach Allen hurt his hamstring and cornerback Pat Surtain II has missed three straight games with an ankle injury.

The Broncos may have scored 30 points against the Cardinals, but this team still has a Bo Nix problem. He scored on a 62-yard run of his own and threw a short pass that RB R.J. Harvey turned into a 52-yard score. But other than that, the Broncos quarterback was once again unimpressive and downright shaky. Maybe this is just the way it’s going to be. The Broncos are just going to keep finding a way to win. But Nix is probably going to have to get it together at some point — like, perhaps, next Sunday against the Chiefs.

Finally, the Denver Broncos got a little juice instead of being held back by the quarterback position.

Bo Nix opened up the Broncos offense with a 62-yard touchdown run. More importantly, the third-year quarterback began to push the ball downfield more against the Arizona Cardinals than he did during Denver’s previous six games.

As a result, the Broncos built a halftime lead and continued to score on their first three second-half drives.

The performance was a welcome change of pace after Denver struggled to get anything going during the first half of previous contests, which makes the Broncos a more complete team as the season progresses.

text:
What started as a slip has turned into a spiral for the 2-5 Eagles, who have now dropped five straight games with a roster that is battered and bruised.

And that’s reflected in the national power rankings, where the Eagles sit among the bottom 10 teams in the NFL following a 38-21 loss to their division rival Dallas Cowboys on Monday.

The Eagles have another NFC East matchup against the Commanders on Sunday Night Football (8:20 p.m., NBC). Here’s how they rank across several outlets heading into Week 8.

ESPN: 23rd

Moving down two spots, the Eagles fell to 23rd on the ESPN Power Rankings.

And even though there has been a lot that has gone wrong for the Eagles, ESPN’s Tim McManus sees a bright spot in the Eagles offense: Wide receiver Dontayvion Wicks, who they acquired in April through a trade with the Packers.

» READ MORE: Jalen Carter, Jordan Davis and an Eagles D-line that was torn apart by the Cowboys

“He quickly established himself as the No. 2 wideout behind DeVonta Smith, ranked second on the team in receiving yards (284), first in catches that resulted in a first down (16) and tied for first in receptions of 20-plus yards (three),” McManus wrote. “An ankle injury sidelined him for Monday night’s game against the Cowboys.”

Monday night was the first game Wicks has missed this season and he is listed as questionable for Week 8.

The Athletic: 23rd

With Halloween on Saturday, The Athletic was celebrating early by finding something spooky with each team in its power rankings. The Eagles, who fell from 20th last week to 23rd, gave Josh Kendall and Chad Graff a lot to choose from.

The Birds may have even presented Graff and Kendall with too many options, leaving them with no choice but to name “this whole season” as the scariest thing about the Eagles right now.

“Make it five straight defeats in a season that’s quickly unraveling following the loss of Jalen Hurts,” Graff and Kendall wrote. “The offense is a shell of its former self. Even the Vic Fangio-led defense struggled on Monday night, forcing just two punts from the Cowboys, while allowing more than 400 yards of offense.”

Bleacher Report: 24th

Bleacher Report moved the Eagles down one spot to 24th heading into Sunday’s matchup against the Commanders.

Moe Moton was quick to point out how the Eagles remained competitive with backup quarterback Tanner McKee, who appeared more comfortable against the Cowboys.

“Philadelphia is in a lost season, though,” Moton wrote. “McKee won’t salvage it, and Saquon Barkley couldn’t finish the game because of a back injury. The Eagles are free-falling in the power rankings following a fifth consecutive loss, and they should be sellers at the trade deadline.”

» READ MORE: Murphy: Vic Fangio had no answers for the Cowboys’ run game, which raises questions for an Eagles team on the brink

Yahoo! Sports: 26th

Yahoo! Sports is the only outlet on this list that has the Birds moving up in the rankings, with a small bump from the 27th spot last week.

But that didn’t mean Frank Schwab was holding back in his assessment of a team “that started the season with legitimate hope of being a Super Bowl contender” and now ”could end up with a top-five draft pick in April."

“There is still enough talent on the roster to be competitive in games, but the effort in the second half against Dallas wasn’t inspiring,” Schwab wrote. “Young teams can sometimes play well in the second half of the season as they keep fighting, like the Saints did last season. That usually doesn’t happen for teams that have recently won a championship, were expected to compete for another this season and are already out of the race before the end of October.”

NFL.com: 28th

The lowest ranking from the Eagles this week came from NFL.com’s Nick Shook, who has Philly as a bottom five team at 28th, for the second week in a row.

text:
GREEN BAY, Wis. (AP) — Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs’ season debut showed that he couldn’t instantly solve all of the problems with the NFL’s lowest-ranked rushing attack.

Now that he has a game under his belt, Jacobs is confident that he has shaken off the rust that came from missing the first six games of the season while on the commissioner’s exempt list. The three-time Pro Bowl selection says it’s imperative for the running backs to play more physically as Green Bay adjusts to injuries on its offensive line.

“Sometimes you’re going to have to break them tackles and you’re going to have to keep your feet running,” Jacobs said Tuesday. “You’ve got to give guys the energy and the juice to feel like you’re carrying it. It could be a bad play. You got a pile and you push the pile or whatever. That’s stuff that gets guys energized and ready to go play.”

Jacobs rushed for 36 yards on 11 carries and caught five passes for 55 yards in a 20-17 loss at Detroit that marked his first game since pleading no contest last month to misdemeanor charges of battery and criminal damage to property stemming from a May altercation with his then-girlfriend.

With the Packers driving for a potential go-ahead score on Sunday, Jacobs couldn’t hang on to a pass in the end zone with the score tied and about 3 1/2 minutes left.

“I felt like I beat him so early (that) when I saw the ball, I kind of tried to slow down for the ball, but that’s a play that literally hit both hands,” Jacobs said. “Whenever it hit any hand, for my standard, I feel like you’ve got to catch it.”

The Packers (4-3) are counting on Jacobs to boost a running game that has struggled heading into Thursday night’s game against the Carolina Panthers (3-3).

Green Bay’s 59.9 yards rushing per game are nearly 15 fewer than anyone else.

The only other team in the past 35 seasons to average fewer than 60 yards per rushing through its first seven games was the 2019 Cincinnati Bengals with 53.1.

Considering those numbers, it’s remarkable that Green Bay is above .500. Since 1933, the other 13 teams that averaged below 60 yards rushing through their seven games went a combined 11-79-1 during that stretch.

“If we want to be the team we want to be, we’ve definitely got to improve the run game,” quarterback Jordan Love said.

Carolina could be just what the Packers need.

The Panthers are coming a 43-13 home loss to Tampa Bay in which they allowed the Buccaneers to rush for 258 yards. Green Bay’s season rushing total didn’t reach 258 yards until its fifth game of the season.

But an offensive line decimated by injuries could have trouble creating running room.

Starting center Sean Rhyan (ankle) and backup Jacob Monk (quadriceps) got hurt against Detroit, with Monk landing on injured reserve. Packers coach Matt LaFleur said it’s uncertain whether Rhyan might end up on injured reserve as well.

Green Bay’s center for most of the Lions game was John Williams, who had never played a single snap on offense in his two-year career before Sunday.

Right guard Travis Glover has a knee issue that leaves his status uncertain for Thursday. The Packers already lost right tackle Zach Bako-Bewele to a season-ending knee injury last month.

All those offensive line injuries could make Jacobs’ job tougher. He’s ready to pick up the slack by gaining yards after contact.

“We’ve still got to make plays, and that’s a part of it,” Jacobs said. “Breaking tackles, grinding out those hard yards … turning a 2-yard run into a 4-yard run. That’s things that motivate the guys and also motivate the play-caller. So that’s something that we’ve definitely got to do.”

NOTES: LaFleur said LB Zaire Franklin (shin) will miss a second straight game Thursday. … WR Matthew Golden is on Green Bay’s injury report with shoulder and foot issues. Although the Packers had a walk-through Tuesday and didn’t practice Monday, the Packers estimated that Golden would have been held out each of those days. … LaFleur was asked about the possibility All-Pro edge rusher Micah Parsons could return to practice next week as he continues his recovery from a torn anterior cruciate ligament. “I sure hope so,” LaFleur said.

AP Pro Football Writer Josh Dubow contributed to this report.

text:
Week 7 Updates

*Updated Tuesday, October 27, 2026

Broken bones, bad knees, pulled muscles, and a few injuries that still have doctors looking for answers. Week 7 took its toll across the NFL, with Chicago losing tight end Cole Kmet for the season and Philadelphia running back Saquon Barkley's return from injury lasting just nine snaps. Even turf toe made an appearance, reminding everyone that sometimes, the smallest body parts can cause the biggest headaches.

Barkley waited two weeks to get back on the football field. It took just one carry for something else to go wrong. The Eagles running back felt his back tighten during a run against Dallas on Monday night and tried to play through it before leaving for good in the third quarter. Philadelphia's official recap described a hamstring strain, but Barkley said afterward that his hamstring felt fine and his back was the problem. He was optimistic about his recovery.

Kmet hurt his right knee after making a catch against New England on Thursday and had to be carted off. Coach Ben Johnson confirmed Friday that his season was over. Minnesota running back Aaron Jones Sr. aggravated a knee injury against Indianapolis, but Monday brought better news. Jones reportedly avoided serious new damage and is considered day-to-day. Carolina's Taylor Moton had barely gotten back on the field after treatment for blood clots in his lungs when a broken fibula sent him right back to the sidelines. He's on injured reserve, along with Green Bay center Jacob Monk.

And there were plenty of other names on the injury report. By the time the NFL put Week 7 in the books Monday night, the injury reports were getting crowded. And for a few teams, the biggest question wasn't who won or lost. It was who'd be healthy enough to suit up next week.

Saquon BarkleyRB · Philadelphia Eagles

Read: Back Injury

Back

Saquon Barkley waited two weeks to get back on the football field after a hamstring injury. His back started giving him trouble on his first carry, a 29-yard run against Dallas. He tried to play through the discomfort, but the pain grew worse as the game continued. Barkley took his final snap in the third quarter and was listed as questionable to return with a back injury early in the fourth. He never got back into the game, finishing with 62 rushing yards and a touchdown on seven carries, along with two catches for nine yards. He was on the field for just nine snaps and touched the ball on every one. Philadelphia's official game recap described the play as a hamstring strain, but Barkley told reporters afterward that his hamstring felt good and identified his back as the problem. He expressed optimism about his recovery.

Recovery Timeline

The Eagles haven't announced a specific back diagnosis, but Barkley's description of tightness offers some hope that this won't be a lengthy absence. If it's a minor muscle problem, rest and treatment could have him feeling better within days. The bigger test will come when he tries to practice at full speed and finds out whether his back can handle the strain.

Injury Risk

Your back does a lot more work than you might think when you're running with a football. It helps keep your body steady when you cut, twist away from a defender, or take a hard hit. When a player is coming off a hamstring injury, there's also the possibility he's moving a little differently to protect that leg, putting extra stress on his back. That doesn't mean Barkley's hamstring caused the tightness, but it's something the Eagles' trainers will want to watch, especially for a running back who relies on sudden bursts of speed and sharp cuts.

Cole KmetTE · Chicago Bears

Read: Knee Injury

Knee

Cole Kmet caught an eight-yard pass against New England and was tackled low along the sideline. His right knee took the hit, and he couldn't put weight on that leg. He was carted off the field, and the Bears confirmed Friday that he won't play again this season. The team has not said exactly what was damaged.

Recovery Timeline

Kmet's season is over, but we don't know yet how long his full recovery will take. If he needs surgery to repair a torn ligament, he could face many months of rehab before he's ready to play again.

Injury Risk

A knee injury doesn't tell us whether Kmet damaged a ligament, the padding inside the joint, or more than one part of the knee. A hard hit can leave the joint swollen and too weak to run, plant, or change direction. Without knowing exactly what was damaged, there's no sound way to predict when his knee will be ready for football again.

Malik Muhammad IICB · Chicago Bears

Read: Foot Injury

Toe

Malik Muhammad II hurt his toe in the third quarter against New England after breaking up a pass. He was listed as doubtful to return and didn't make it back into the game. The Bears have not said whether the toe is sprained or broken.

Recovery Timeline

A minor toe injury may settle down with a few days of rest. A bad sprain or broken toe can take several weeks to heal, and Muhammad needs to be able to push off that foot before he can cover receivers again.

Injury Risk

Think about what a cornerback does on every pass play. He's moving backward, turning, and taking off after someone running full speed. His toes help him push off and keep his balance through all of that. Even a small injury can cost him a step, and in the NFL, that's often all a receiver needs.

Taylor MotonT · Carolina Panthers

Read: Leg Injury

Broken Fibula

Taylor Moton was blocking against Tampa Bay when teammate Rasheed Walker fell across the back of his legs. Moton went down and had to be carted off. Coach Dave Canales confirmed that he'd broken his left fibula, and Carolina placed him on injured reserve Monday. The timing makes this one especially tough. Moton had missed the first four games while recovering from blood clots in his lungs and had only returned to the field a week earlier against Philadelphia. After months of treatment and working his way back into football shape, he made it through just two games before another serious injury put him back on the sideline.

Recovery Timeline

Moton must miss at least four games under NFL injured-reserve rules. A broken fibula often takes six to eight weeks to heal, sometimes longer. And that's before he can think about planting that leg and holding off a 300-pound defender, especially if the break requires surgery.

Injury Risk

The fibula is the smaller bone on the outside of your lower leg. It helps support the ankle and keep the leg steady. Some breaks heal with a cast or boot, while others need surgery to hold the bone in place. For a lineman who spends every snap pushing against another big man, the bone must be strong enough to handle an awful lot of force.

Aaron Jones Sr.RB · Minnesota Vikings

Read: MCL Injury

MCL

Aaron Jones Sr. took a low hit at the end of a 17-yard run against Indianapolis and hurt his left knee again. He's been playing with a sprained MCL since Week 2, so the Vikings feared he might have made it worse. But Monday brought better news. The injury isn't believed to be serious, and Jones is now considered day-to-day.

Recovery Timeline

A mild MCL sprain often heals in one to three weeks, while a worse sprain may take four to six weeks or longer. Jones has already played through this injury for several weeks, so the big question is whether Sunday's hit caused more damage or just brought back the pain.

Injury Risk

The MCL is a strong band of tissue on the inside of your knee. It keeps the joint from bending too far sideways. A hit to the outside of the leg can stretch or tear it. That's a problem for a running back who needs to plant one foot, change direction, and burst through a hole before it closes.

Sean RhyanC · Green Bay Packers

Read: Ankle Injury

Ankle

Sean Rhyan hurt his left ankle on Green Bay's first offensive series against Detroit when running back Josh Jacobs and a defender rolled into the back of his leg. He didn't return. NFL Network reported Monday that Rhyan is believed to have suffered a high ankle sprain, which is more troublesome than a common ankle sprain.

Recovery Timeline

Rhyan is expected to miss Thursday's game against Carolina, and Green Bay is reportedly considering placing him on injured reserve. High ankle sprains can take four to six weeks or longer to heal, depending on the damage, but the Packers have not announced a firm timetable.

Injury Risk

A high ankle sprain hurts the band of tissue that holds the two lower-leg bones together just above the ankle. Unlike a common ankle sprain, the damage is higher up, where the two bones need to stay steady as the player puts weight on his foot. For a center who has to brace against a defensive tackle, every snap puts pressure on that injured area.

Jacob MonkC/G · Green Bay Packers

Read: Leg Injury

Quadriceps

Jacob Monk came in after Sean Rhyan got hurt but didn't last long. He injured his quadriceps muscle in the first quarter against Detroit, forcing Green Bay to turn to John Williams at center. Monk had already missed several games earlier this season with a quadriceps injury, and Sunday's setback put him back on the sideline. The Packers placed him on injured reserve Monday and signed veteran guard Mekhi Becton Sr. from their practice squad to take his roster spot.

Recovery Timeline

Monk must miss at least four games, meaning he won't be eligible to return until after Green Bay's next four contests. A mild quadriceps strain may improve within a few weeks, but a more serious injury can take longer. Because Monk had already been dealing with trouble in that muscle, the Packers will want to make sure it's strong enough before he returns.

Injury Risk

The quadriceps are four muscles on the front of the thigh that help straighten the knee and push off the ground. A quadriceps injury may be a strained muscle or a bruise caused by a hard blow. With a bruise, there's a lot of stiffness. Green Bay hasn't said which kind Monk suffered, but either one can make blocking a 300-pound defender a difficult job.

Erick All Jr.TE · Cincinnati Bengals

Read: Knee Injury

Knee

Erick All Jr. hurt his right knee while making a catch against Baltimore in the third quarter. He left the game and was ruled out. It's especially concerning because All has already undergone multiple surgeries on that same knee during his football career. Coach Zac Taylor said Monday that the Bengals were still gathering information about the injury.

Recovery Timeline

The Bengals have not said what was damaged, so there's no firm date for his return. A mild sprain might heal in a few weeks, but a torn ligament or damaged cartilage could mean a much longer stay on the sideline.

Injury Risk

All has already been through the work of rebuilding an injured knee. Another injury to that joint raises questions about how much damage it can handle. Torn ligaments can make a knee unstable, while damaged cartilage can cause swelling or make the joint catch when it bends. Doctors will want to know exactly what happened before deciding how much football that knee can safely take.

Rashid ShaheedWR · Seattle Seahawks

Read: Knee Injury

Knee

Rashid Shaheed collided with teammate Jaxon Smith-Njigba on a pass that Kansas City picked off just before halftime. He didn't play in the second half and was later ruled out with a knee injury. On Monday, Seattle coach Mike Macdonald said the early results looked positive, although he wasn't ready to say when Shaheed would return.

Recovery Timeline

Seattle still needs to know exactly what happened inside that knee. If the injury is only a bruise or mild sprain, Shaheed may not miss much time.

Injury Risk

Speed is a big part of Shaheed's game, and his knees take a beating when he hits top gear, stops, or makes someone miss. Pain or swelling can rob him of the quick first step that makes him dangerous. Even if nothing is torn, the Seahawks need to know he can run at full speed before putting him back on the field. A more serious ligament injury could keep him out much longer.

Charles CrossT · Seattle Seahawks

Read: Ankle Sprain

High Ankle Sprain

Charles Cross left Seattle's win over Kansas City in the fourth quarter and didn't return. NFL Network reported Monday that Cross suffered a high ankle sprain. Josh Jones finished the game at left tackle.

Recovery Timeline

Seattle reportedly hopes Cross can return in one or two weeks, although high ankle sprains can take considerably longer to heal. His progress will depend on how much the injury affects his ability to move sideways and hold his ground while blocking.

Injury Risk

A high ankle sprain can make twisting and pushing off painful because the injured tissue sits between the two lower-leg bones. Players can have different amounts of swelling and recover at different speeds. That's why Cross might return sooner than expected or need more time, depending on how his ankle heals.

Week 6 Updates

*Updated Tuesday, October 20, 2026

A kicker makes a tackle and loses his season. A veteran receiver pulls up on a route with nobody near him. A rookie linebacker leaves on a stretcher, then walks back into his team's locker room a few hours later.

Sunday was another reminder that the distance between a routine NFL play and a trip to the training room can be awfully short.

By Monday, the Los Angeles Rams had received some of the worst news. Kicker Blake Grupe tore his ACL in his first game with the team. Receiver Davante Adams suffered a ruptured hamstring that will sideline him for six to 10 weeks.

In Atlanta, the outlook was considerably brighter. Falcons linebacker Kendal Daniels returned to the team facility after a frightening neck injury sent him to a hospital Sunday afternoon.

Elsewhere, teams were still sorting through ankle injuries, damaged shoulders, concussions, and the uncertainty that comes when an injured player leaves the stadium without a firm diagnosis.

Here's what happened during Sunday's games, what changed Monday, and what each injury means for the work they'll have to do before returning to the field.

Jalen HurtsQB · Philadelphia Eagles

Blood Clots

The Eagles quarterback was injured during Philadelphia's Oct. 4 loss to the Los Angeles Rams but continued practicing. An ultrasound performed in London on Oct. 10 revealed a superficial blood clot in his left calf.

Team physicians determined Hurts could safely play against Jacksonville the following day. He completed 21 of 40 passes for 220 yards and a touchdown in a 19-17 loss.

A follow-up ultrasound raised new concerns, prompting additional medical evaluation. Hurts was ruled out against Carolina and placed on injured reserve Oct. 17.

By Monday, Oct. 19, additional testing revealed deep vein thrombosis and blood clots in both lungs.

Recovery Timeline

Approximately six months or longer, depending on treatment and medical clearance.

Blood thinners help prevent existing clots from growing and reduce the risk of new ones forming while the body gradually breaks down the clots already present.

Treatment for DVT and pulmonary embolism commonly lasts at least three months, sometimes longer. NFL reporting indicates Hurts' treatment is expected to take approximately three months.

He can continue appropriate conditioning, but contact football must wait until doctors determine that anticoagulation can safely end and he receives medical clearance.

Injury Risk

Blood clots aren't something most fans associate with an NFL quarterback, but they can affect anyone, including elite athletes.

DVT occurs when a clot forms in a deep vein, usually in the leg. If part of that clot breaks loose, it can travel to the lungs and obstruct blood flow.

That's a pulmonary embolism, and it can be life-threatening.

In Hurts' case, doctors found clots in both lungs.

There is an important distinction between the superficial clot initially identified in London and the more serious diagnosis announced Monday. Superficial clots form in veins closer to the skin. Deep vein clots carry a greater risk of pulmonary embolism.

The precise progression of Hurts' condition has not been publicly established.

Reed BlankenshipS · Houston Texans

Read: What Is a Concussion?

Concussion

Reed Blankenship's afternoon in London ended before halftime.

The Texans safety took a hit to the head late in the first half against Jacksonville and was taken to the locker room for evaluation. An independent neurological consultant determined he had suffered a concussion, ruling him out of play for the rest of the game, which Houston won, 34-31.

M.J. Stewart moved into the secondary alongside Calen Bullock as Houston finished the game without Blankenship.

Recovery Timeline

Doctors don’t have a fixed number of days they use for predicting a player’s return after a concussion or head trauma. Just like the symptoms, recovery can vary widely from person to person. One athlete might become symptom-free quickly, while another could still have symptoms several weeks later.

Symptoms that last for more than four weeks are considered "persisting," and a player may need further medical testing.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 278 studies on concussion recovery found that it took an average of 14 days until athletes were symptom-free after concussion. It also took an average of 19.8 days until they were able to return to their sport. Researchers found that, in general, the worse the initial symptoms, the longer the return-to-sport time was.

Injury Risk

Safeties spend much of their game day closing ground on receivers and running backs. That means frequent collisions, often with both players moving at considerable speed.

Concussions can result from direct head contact or forces that cause the brain to accelerate rapidly inside the skull.

The NFL recorded 538 in-game concussion evaluations during the 2025 season. Those were evaluations, not 538 confirmed concussions, but the number illustrates how closely the league monitors potential head injuries.

For Blankenship, returning to practice is only one step. Returning to contact requires neurological clearance.

Tony AdamsS · Tennessee Titans

Read: Ankle Injury

Ankle Injury

Tennessee beat Indianapolis, 26-20, but safety Tony Adams couldn't finish the game.

Adams injured an ankle during the fourth quarter and was unable to return. The Titans did not identify the specific play or disclose whether the injury involved ligaments, tendons, or another structure.

For a safety, an unreliable ankle can affect the two things he needs most: closing speed and the ability to change direction.

Recovery Timeline

Recovery time varies. An ankle injury can keep an athlete out for a few days or weeks, but more serious injuries can lead to a much longer absence.

How long a player is unable to play depends on many different things, including:

Exact diagnosis and how severe the injury is

Whether the joint is stable

Whether surgery is needed

The player’s position

How pain, swelling, and other symptoms are managed

When strength and range of motion are regained

Medical clearance

Injury Risk

Ankles take considerable punishment in football. Players get rolled up in traffic, twist their feet beneath falling bodies, and change direction while carrying their full weight on one leg.

A conventional lateral ankle sprain and a high-ankle sprain involve different ligaments and can have significantly different recovery periods.

Two ankle injuries can look remarkably similar Sunday night and produce very different practice reports by Wednesday.

Nolan SmithDE · Philadelphia Eagles

Read: What Is a Concussion?

Concussion

Nolan Smith was coming off the edge with 12:45 remaining in the second quarter against Carolina when Panthers running back Chuba Hubbard delivered a chip block.

Smith went down, was checked for a concussion, and did not return.

The Eagles lost their edge rusher in a game they eventually dropped, 25-14. Smith had already recorded a sack, his third of the season, before the injury ended his afternoon.

Philadelphia was already playing without several important offensive starters, and losing another pass rusher added to its problems.

Recovery Timeline

Doctors don’t have a fixed number of days they use for predicting a player’s return after a concussion or head trauma. Just like the symptoms, recovery can vary widely from person to person. One athlete might become symptom-free quickly, while another could still have symptoms several weeks later.

Symptoms that last for more than four weeks are considered "persisting," and a player may need further medical testing.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 278 studies on concussion recovery found that it took an average of 14 days until athletes were symptom-free after a concussion. It also took an average of 19.8 days until they were able to return to their sport. Researchers found that, in general, the worse the initial symptoms, the longer the return-to-sport time was.

Injury Risk

Pass rushers face contact from more than offensive tackles. Running backs and tight ends routinely deliver chip blocks to slow defenders before releasing into pass routes.

Those hits can arrive while a defender is focused on the quarterback.

A concussion doesn't require a player to lose consciousness. Headaches, confusion, dizziness, balance problems, and slowed reactions can all indicate trouble.

The league's protocol is designed to keep players from returning before those neurological problems have resolved.

Carson SteeleRB · Philadelphia Eagles

Read: Shoulder Injury

Shoulder Injury

Carson Steele caught a short pass from Tanner McKee during the first quarter against Carolina and was pushed out of bounds, injuring his shoulder.

He visited the medical tent, briefly returned on special teams in the second quarter, then underwent another evaluation and was ruled out.

The injury further thinned an Eagles backfield already missing Saquon Barkley, Tank Bigsby, and Will Shipley.

Recovery Timeline

Shoulder injury recovery time varies. A shoulder injury can keep an athlete out for a few days or weeks, but more serious injuries can lead to a much longer absence.

A dislocated shoulder, for example, can be relatively minor or be so serious it requires surgery to repair. For minor or simple dislocations, once the shoulder is put back into the correct position, a return to the field may be possible within a few weeks. If surgery is necessary for an unstable shoulder, a full recovery that includes physical therapy could take up to nine months.

While timetables are often used to project a player’s recovery, his actual recovery period may be longer or shorter, depending on several things, such as how the player responds to various tests of strength, stability, and pain-free range of motion.

Other things to look at include time since the injury, physical examinations of the shoulder, and the results of X-rays, MRIs, and other imaging.

Injury Risk

Shoulder injuries are familiar territory for NFL running backs, who regularly absorb blows while lowering their bodies into tackles.

The acromioclavicular joint, where the collarbone meets the shoulder, is particularly vulnerable to falls and direct contact.

But a shoulder injury isn't automatically a separation. The damaged structure has to be identified before the team can establish a meaningful recovery plan.

Jordan DavisDT · Philadelphia Eagles

Read: Ankle Injury

Ankle Injury

Davis went down during the fourth quarter against Carolina and needed help getting off the field.

The Eagles defensive tackle was evaluated for an ankle injury and ruled out. Philadelphia did not disclose the specific damage.

For Davis, the concern goes beyond running and changing direction. An interior defensive lineman must generate power from his lower body while absorbing the force of offensive linemen trying to move him.

When an ankle won't support that load, even routine plays become difficult.

Recovery Timeline

Recovery time varies. An ankle injury can keep an athlete out for a few days or weeks, but more serious injuries can lead to a much longer absence.

How long a player is unable to play depends on many different things, including:

Exact diagnosis and how severe the injury is

Whether the joint is stable

Whether surgery is needed

The player’s position

How pain, swelling, and other symptoms are managed

When strength and range of motion are regained

Medical clearance

Injury Risk

The interior line is a crowded workplace. Feet get caught beneath other players, legs get rolled up, and enormous forces are transferred through planted ankles.

For defensive tackles, rehabilitation must account for more than straight-line running. The joint has to withstand repeated contact and powerful lateral movement.

Brandin EcholsCB · Pittsburgh Steelers

Read: Upper Leg Injury

Hamstring Injury

Brandin Echols pulled up while blocking on a Pittsburgh punt return against Tampa Bay late in the second quarter.

The Steelers cornerback began favoring his leg, lost his block, and limped off the field. Pittsburgh subsequently ruled him out with a hamstring injury.

His absence affected both the secondary's depth and the special teams unit.

Recovery Timeline

Recovery time varies by the type of injury and how severe it is. A mild strain or bruise may take only a few days or weeks to heal. Sometimes, players don't miss any game time. A complete tear can take many months of recovery, especially if it requires surgery. A player with a severe injury could miss the whole season.

Recovery time after a fracture is at least a few months. Players may have to wait even longer to return to practice and games. Sometimes, it takes a full year to fully recover and go back to playing.

Don't depend on published averages for a player's recovery and return to play (RTP). These numbers can't accurately predict when an athlete will come back. Return times vary based on:

The type of injury and how severe it is

How well the player heals

The demands of their position

How they respond to treatment

Injury Risk

Hamstrings are among the NFL's most troublesome soft-tissue injuries, particularly for receivers, cornerbacks, and return specialists.

The muscles along the back of the thigh work hard during sprinting and deceleration.

The league reported that hamstring and other lower-extremity strain rates in 2025 were roughly half the levels recorded from 2018 through 2022.

Reinjury remains a concern, especially when players return before full-speed strength has been restored.

Grant DelpitS · Cleveland Browns

Read: What Is a Concussion?

Concussion

Grant Delpit suffered a concussion during the first quarter of Cleveland's 13-10 win over Baltimore.

The Browns safety took a hit while making a tackle, was evaluated, and was ruled out. He finished with two tackles.

A game account indicated the contact involved teammate Derek Barnett, although the Browns' official injury announcement did not specify the collision.

A systematic review and meta-analysis of 278 studies on concussion recovery found that it took an average of 14 days until athletes were symptom-free after concussion. It also took an average of 19.8 days until they were able to return to their sport. Researchers found that, in general, the worse the initial symptoms, the longer the return-to-sport time was.

Injury Risk

Safeties often arrive at tackles with a running start. Even incidental contact can create substantial force when multiple players converge on the ball carrier.

A concussion may occur without a player being knocked unconscious, and symptoms can evolve after the initial impact.

The NFL requires follow-up evaluations after game-day concussion assessments because feeling better right afterward doesn't necessarily mean the brain has recovered.

Greg Newsome IICB · New York Giants

Read: What Is a Concussion?

Concussion

The Giants lost cornerback Greg Newsome II during the third quarter of Sunday's 34-27 loss to New Orleans.

Newsome was evaluated for a concussion and did not return. New York did not publicly identify the specific play responsible.

His departure left the Giants shuffling their defensive backfield as the Saints built a sizable second-half lead.

It also took an average of 19.8 days until they were able to return to their sport. Researchers found that, in general, the worse the initial symptoms, the longer the return-to-sport time was.

Injury Risk

Cornerbacks face high-speed contact while making tackles and competing for passes.

A defender can get a concussion from direct contact with another player's helmet, shoulder, or body, or from striking the ground.

For Newsome, passing a medical examination matters more than being able to run routes during a walkthrough. He must be neurologically ready for contact before returning to coverage.

Darnell MooneyWR · New York Giants

Read: Neck and Back Injuries

Neck Injury

Darnell Mooney left the Giants' loss to New Orleans with a neck injury and did not return.

The team did not identify the specific play or disclose whether the injury involved muscles, ligaments, nerves, or the cervical spine.

Without knowing what's injured, there's no reliable way to predict when Mooney can return.

Recovery Timeline

Recovery time varies widely based on the injury a player has. A player with a stinger may sometimes return during the same game once their symptoms are gone and their examination is normal. But most neck or spine injuries can keep an athlete out for a few days or weeks. More serious injuries can lead to a much longer absence, especially if treatment involves surgery.

Fractures also have a wide range of recovery times, but typically, an athlete will be out for a while to heal.

Injury Risk

Football neck injuries can develop from sudden rotation, impact, or compression.

A common condition called a stinger temporarily affects nerves between the neck and arm, but Mooney has not been diagnosed publicly with one.

Doctors must first establish the source of the symptoms and rule out potentially serious damage before determining when a player can safely return.

text:
The Packers swapped offensive lineman on their active roster on Monday, placing Jacob Monk on injured reserve and promoting Mekhi Becton from the practice squad.

Monk, 25, started Green Bay’s first three games before being benched for Travis Glover. He returned to his backup center role and took the field for Sean Rhyan after he suffered a high ankle sprain during Sunday’s loss to the Lions. Monk only played five snaps before going down with a quadriceps injury that will sideline him for at least four games.

Second-year lineman John Williams, listed as the backup left tackle on the Packers’ depth chart, closed out the game at center, his first in-game snaps at the position in his college or NFL career. His situation is very similar to that of Ravens rookie guard Vega Ioane, who took over at center after Baltimore’s starter and backup went down. Ioane went on to start the next three games, but Williams may not get a similar opportunity with rookie Jager Burton also on the roster. The former Kentucky Wildcat was a healthy scratch in Week 7, but his 15 college starts at center could position him for the starting job until Rhyan is back on the field.

Becton will provide much-needed depth amid the Packers’ growing injury crisis along their offensive line. Right tackle Zach Bako-Bawele is already on IR with a torn patellar tendon that will sideline him for the rest of the season. He has since been joined by Rhyan and Monk. Compounding the problems are additional injuries to Travis Glover and Aaron Banks and a short week before a Thursday night matchup against the Panthers. Glover, currently the starting right guard, missed Monday’s practice with a nee injury, while Banks was limited by a knee/toe issue.

Becton can back up either tackle spot in the event of an injury. That would allow the Packers to reserve their backup center – either Williams or Burton – in case the starter goes down. He could also start in Glover’s place at right guard or take Banks’ role as a backup. His versatility keeps the Packers’ options open as they evaluate their options in the coming days.

text:
EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. -- The New York Giants are placing running back Tyrone Tracy Jr. on injured reserve with a hamstring injury, general manager Joe Schoen announced Tuesday.

Tracy was set to split the majority of the running back reps with Cam Skattebo prior to suffering the injury in Sunday's 27-21 win over the Houston Texans. He left in the first half after logging 10 offensive snaps to Skattebo's 13.

Devin Singletary, who scored the game-winning touchdown in Houston, is expected to play a bigger role in Tracy's absence. The Giants are also signing running back Greg Desrosiers off the practice squad from the Los Angeles Chargers to take Tracy's roster spot.

"We have lots of confidence in [Skattebo] and Singletary," Schoen said. "And we'll have to see what Greg can do."

Schoen did not think Tracy's injury would be long-term, but he still has to miss a minimum of four games.

The Giants (4-2-1) are on their bye week and next play the Philadelphia Eagles on Nov. 7.

It does not appear the Giants are desperate to make a trade for a running back, even though there has been speculation about Indianapolis' Jonathan Taylor being available. Schoen didn't close the door on any potential moves, but he did note that the Giants are short on picks in next year's draft.

The Giants are already without fourth- and fifth-round picks in the 2027 NFL draft.

"We're going to look at all the options that are available and certain teams have already started some trades," Schoen said. "We've been in contact with those teams and have a pretty good idea who may or may not be available. And it's got to make sense short-term and long-term."

Skattebo rushed for a career-high 124 yards (including 97 in the second half) against the Texans after being demoted for the previous game. He didn't have a single carry the prior week in a loss to the New Orleans Saints.

Tracy had scored touchdowns in consecutive weeks prior to the injury. He had a rushing touchdown in the first quarter against the Texans.

The third-year back came into the season expected to share the workload with Skattebo, but a missed block in the preseason that sent quarterback Jaxson Dart to the injury tent and a fumble in the opener against the Dallas Cowboys landed him in the doghouse.

Tracy was relegated to mostly special teams the next few weeks; he had just two carries over the next three games. But he slowly worked himself back into the mix, and he tied his season high with six carries in less than a half of action on Sunday.

Tracy's spirits were high after the dramatic win over Houston and it did not appear the injury was serious. He said he first felt the hamstring during practice earlier in the week.

Tracy, 26, had more than 1,000 all-purpose yards (receiving and rushing) in each of his first two seasons with the Giants. He was a fifth-round pick out of Iowa and has 55 yards and two touchdowns on 19 carries this season.

Was Barkley ready to go?

text:
On his first carry of the Week 4 game against the Rams, Eagles running back Saquon Barkley suffered a hamstring injury. After missing two games, he aggravated it on his first carry of the Week 7 game against the Cowboys.

It raises an obvious question. Was Barkley ready to go? At a deeper level, it’s fair to wonder whether the mutual desire for Barkley to play was driven by the opportunity to find a trade partner for Barkley before the deadline, which arrives in two weeks.

After the loss to Dallas, coach Nick Sirianni was asked about the decision to play Barkley, 22 days after he strained his hamstring.

“Obviously, you saw that he was on a pitch count out there today,” Sirianni told reporters. “There was constant communication to see how he was feeling, see where he was, and obviously, he came out early in the second half. Again, when you go into something like that, you make sure that the player’s health is first and foremost. Is he ready to go? Do they feel ready to go? Do the doctors and trainers feel like they’re ready to go? We felt like that was the case today, but obviously wanted to keep a close eye on him, and he’s tough as heck. He wanted to be out there for his teammates, probably had to slow him [down] as far as -- he’d be out there every play because of the person he is and the teammate he is and the player he is and the toughness that he has.

“So, we tried to be smart with him there, but it was good to have him back out there. He obviously had a nice game and was very productive when he touched the football.”

Things changed after that first carry. He throttled back on the temptation to reach top speed.

“He obviously got out of there on that and did a good job of protecting himself,” Sirianni said regarding Barkley’s first carry. “I think that’s a play that, normally with Saquon, you see him break out of that and it’s hard to catch him in those situations. I mean, you change as you go. Obviously, I think he probably played a little less than what we initially thought. He definitely played a little less than what we initially thought. But like I said, he’s tough as heck and it’s good to have him back out there, just to have his presence out there and then his playmaking ability.”

Eventually, Barkley left the game with what was called a back injury. And that complicates any possibility of finding a contender that will give real value to the Eagles. With Colts running back Jonathan Taylor potentially available, a team looking for a running back will be looking for a player who is as close to healthy as possible.

Vikings who could return in Week 8

Myles Price, WR

He was cleared to return to the game, but head coach Kevin O'Connell did say that Price was dealing with a stinger after the win. Jordan Addison, WR

Aaron Jones Sr., RB

Vikings out for the season

Luckily, the Vikings didn't appear to lose anyone to a long-term injury on Sunday. The key Vikings out for the season remained the same with Donovan Jackson, Josh Oliver, Jamal Adams and Tyler Batty all already lost for the year.

text:
A major theme this season has been the Vikings' patience with their 2026 rookie class. While those rookies are growing and developing, the Purple and Gold have relied on their more experienced players on the roster to be major contributors.

That philosophy has had an interesting impact on first-round pick Caleb Banks and third-round pick Domonique Orange, who were selected to eventually replace last year's starters—Jonathan Allen and Javon Hargrave—after they were both released back in the offseason.

Former United Football League standout Jalen Redmond is having a fantastic season on Minnesota's defensive line and played 54 of Minnesota's 59 defensive snaps in Week 7. Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins had the next most defensive line snaps, playing 46 reps.

Banks and Orange played 12 and 13 defensive snaps, respectively, in Sunday's victory over the Colts. Since the Vikings are bringing them along slowly, the lower snap counts make sense from a development perspective.

However, Banks limped off the field against the Colts after being down and did not return to action. If he is forced to miss time with that injury, this could be an opportunity for "Big Citrus" to set more defensive work against the Lions in Week 8.

Domonique Orange suddenly looks a lot more important for the Vikings

Orange has played 91 defensive snaps this year for Minnesota. Although he participates on special teams as well, he has four tackles this season, with one of those being for a loss against the Packers in the season opener. His 42.9 defense grade on Pro Football Focus is far from ideal, but three of his last four performances were higher than that mark. He's also averaged a run-defense grade of 57.4 in the last games after averaging 46.1 in the first two.

Assuming he doesn't play on Sunday, the 15.7 defensive snaps that Banks averages per game could be up for grabs.

Some of those could go to Orange, and if he can get about 25 defensive snaps against the Lions on Sunday, it could show how much he has developed since joining the team. That would be his career-high defensive snap count, besting his 24 reps against the Bears in Week 2.

The Lions run the fourth-most offensive players per game (66.3), so there should be more than enough opportunities to get on the field.

Developing Orange is even more important when looking at the long-term value of the defensive lineman. While staying on top of the NFC North or remaining undefeated is great, this team is in position to potentially be a scary playoff team, and having him as an asset to rotate into defensive coordinator Brian Flores's squad would be extremely valuable.

At only 22 years old, Orange should have a long NFL career in front of him. Getting him experience and evaluating his development in Week 8 could go a long way in preparing the young defender for a long and prosperous tenure with the Vikings.
