text:
Hinshaw partner Scott Seaman was recently quoted in Law360 Insurance Authority, examining the significance of a New York appellate court’s ruling regarding how many “occurrences” are involved for purposes of insurance coverage for the National Football League’s (NFL) concussion litigation settlement.

What the Court Ruled

Earlier this month, New York’s Appellate Division, First Judicial Department, held that each former player’s alleged injury was at least one separate occurrence.

Because of that ruling, the excess insurer does not have to indemnify the NFL for the uncapped multidistrict litigation settlement with former players.

Its fifth-layer policy covered a portion of any loss exceeding $51 million. The court said coverage would instead fall under a primary policy issued for the same 2001–2002 policy period.

The Ruling’s Implications on Insurance Coverage Litigation

Scott explained that a party’s position on the number of occurrences often depends on where its policy sits in the coverage program. “As this case illustrates, where a party stands on the number of occurrences issue may depend upon where it sits on the coverage chart.”

He also said the court’s decision shows that the number of occurrences is still a major issue in insurance litigation. Coverage turns on the size of the loss, where each policy attaches, and whether aggregate limits apply.

Additionally, Scott noted that the First Judicial Department applied New York’s “unfortunate event” test in a straightforward way. “Although the claims shared some commonalities, the claims of over 20,000 former players who participated in approximately 10,000 games over multiple decades in approximately 90 different stadiums did not share the same ‘temporal and spatial’ characteristics to unify them as one occurrence,” he explained.

text:
Detroit Lions coach Dan Campbell gave a couple of injury updates in his Monday afternoon press conference, and it's mostly good news.

Let's start with Amon-Ra St. Brown. I'm guessing many weren't aware St. Brown was even dealing with an injury, as he never exited the game and wasn't given a specific injury designation on Sunday. However, Detroit Football Network's Justin Rogers noted that the Lions did not make him available in the locker room because he was getting treatment for a swollen ankle.

Campbell said they expect to sit St. Brown for Wednesday's practice, but they're optimistic he'll be okay and are hoping he'll be ready to go for Thursday.

"He and Ennis (Rakestraw), I think those guys will probably sit Wednesday, but the plan is to get them going Thursday, and I think that they'll be fine. They should be good," Campbell said, before adding. "Now, we'll see when we get there, but—yep."

St. Brown is coming off his best game of the season, hauling in nine catches for a season-high 153 yards. That's the fifth-most yards he's had in a single game for his career. Obviously, missing him would be a big deal, but Campbell doesn't sound too concerned at the moment.

The Lions are expecting the same trajectory for cornerback Ennis Rakestraw, who did leave the game early with an ankle injury.

"It's not major, he's got a little ankle here," Campbell said. "We feel like, as of right now, he'll be at practice on Thursday. That's kinda what we're looking at. But we don't feel like it's major as of today."

Rakestraw was part of a pretty massive cornerback rotation against the Packers. Rakestraw (21 snaps) shared playing time with D.J. Reed (61), Roger McCreary (67), Rock Ya-Sin (14), and Khalil Dorsey (14). It was a game plan inspired by the Dallas Cowboys' attack against the Packers to keep the players fresh. Campbell said it's an approach they will continue to consider moving forward.

"I think there was also merit for a number of those guys plays," Campbell said. "Letting them all kinda play, getting some reps and using them in different situations, different packages."

text:
Seattle Seahawks left tackle Charles Cross is expected to miss time after an MRI revealed that he suffered a high ankle sprain in the team's win over the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday night, a source told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

A source told Rapoport that the hope is Cross can return in one or two weeks.

Cross limped off the field in the fourth quarter and did not return. Josh Jones finished the game and is now in line to start the Seahawks' Week 8 game against the Chicago Bears on "Monday Night Football."

The Seahawks also lost wide receiver Rashid Shaheed to a knee injury Sunday that kept him out of the second half. On his Seattle Sports 710-AM radio show Monday, coach Mike Macdonald said, "the early returns are positive."

Macdonald also said on his radio show that the Seahawks will open up the 21-day practice window this week on rookie running back Jadarian Price, who has spent the past four games on injured reserve due to a chest injury.

Price, the team's first-round pick, is one half of their desired backfield duo along with Zach Charbonnet, who has yet to make his season debut following February ACL surgery. Charbonnet was inactive Sunday after a full week of participation in practice.

"We're sticking to our plan where he's still going to practice in a full capacity and then we'll evaluate as the week goes on and go from there," Macdonald said.

text:
The Houston Texans got hit with a reality check in their Week 7 loss vs. the New York Giants, as they would end up falling short in an overtime defeat, 21-27 that now sinks them to a 2-5 record on the year heading into the bye.

However, it seems the Texans were also hit with a key injury in their wide receiver room in the midst of their Week 7 loss, according to head coach DeMeco Ryans.

And that injury was to none other than second-year wide receiver Jaylin Noel, who ended up leaving in the middle of Sunday's contest against the Giants before inevitably being unable to return.

What DeMeco Ryans Said About Jaylin Noel's Injury

Per DeMeco Ryans' post-game press conference following Houston's loss vs. the Giants, the Texans' head coach revealed that Noel had suffered a turf toe injury against New York.

"Jaylin Noel had a turf toe injury. He's still being evaluated," Ryans said on Sunday.

Obviously, there's not a ton of information that we can gather from Ryans' post-game comments when it comes to Noel's status moving forward. However, a turf toe injury––depending on the exact severity––is one that can lead to some missed time for any player in the league.

Noel finished the game against the Giants with just two receptions for a loss of three yards. According to KPRC2's Aaron Wilson, Noel was also reportedly in a walking boot following the Texans' loss.

The good news for the Texans is that they'll be heading right into their bye week following the events of their Week 7 loss. Which means, for Noel, he'll have an extra week of rest to bank on before he'll be tasked with suiting up for Houston's next game.

However, even with that extra time off, there's a chance that Noel could be due to miss some time for the Texans moving forward–– which would undoubtably be a big loss to Houston's offense knowing how strong of a start to the season the second-year wideout has had through seven weeks.

Through the start of the Texans' season, Noel has put together a total of 19 receptions for 331 yards and two receptions, really becoming one of the team's most noteworthy playmakers in the passing game, even with the immense depth that's come to surround him in the wide receiver room.

His ability as a downfield playmaker, someone who can excel after the catch, and even as a kick returner has shown up big in his second year pro. Yet, depending on just how bad his new turf toe injury might be, there's a chance the Texans will be forced to push ahead without him for a few games moving forward.

If Noel is due to miss any time for the Texans' offense, C.J. Stroud will be forced to lean on some other playmakers in this wide receiver room that does have the depth to support a solid offense, even without the second-year talent.

Keep an eye on the obvious candidates of Nico Collins and Marvin Harrison Jr. to likely see more responsibilities in the Texans' offense in the weeks ahead.

Yet, you can also expect guys like Kayshon Boutte, Xavier Hutchinson, and Tank Dell to step up and provide the playmaking this offense could desperately utilize without one of their more potent names at the position group altogether.

We'll likely know more on Noel's long-term status a bit better once we get to next week's practice leading up to the Texans' Week 9 battle vs. the Los Angeles Chargers. However, certainly brace for the possibility that this offense could be without Noel for some stretch of time, depending on how bad the toe injury is truly deemed to be.

title: Gamechanger for Excess Insurer: Court Concludes NFL Player Concussion Claims ... - Tressler LLP
description:
AIGLIC issued the fifth layer excess liability policy to the NFL that followed form to the TIG primary Policy.
The AIGLIC Policy provided the same coverage for damages covered by the TIG Policy.
The court also overturned the Supreme Court’s finding that NFL football was a “product” under the PCOH coverage.
The lower court had concluded the term “product” could, as a matter of “common speech” include intangible items like NFL football.
“The plain language indicates that the product, as expected to be covered by the PCOH, is a tangible/physical product.
text:
In 2014, the National Football League and NFL Properties, LLC (together, NFL) entered into a class action settlement in federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) resolving litigation brought by former players alleging the NFL failed to inform them of and protect them from concussion risks in football. Coverage litigation began long before the settlement was inked. On October 1, 2026, the coverage dispute inched closer to final resolution with the decision of the New York Appellate Division in Discover Prop. & Cas. Co., et al. v. Nat’l Football League, et al. —N.Y.S.3d —, No. 2025-03200, 2026 WL 2948933 (N.Y. App. Div. Oct. 1, 2026). The Appellate Division reversed key rulings entered by the New York Supreme Court, New York County, on cross-motions for summary judgment, finding each claim by or on behalf of a former player constitutes at least one “occurrence” under a primary policy issued by TIG Insurance Company (TIG) and that NFL football is not a “product” as that term is defined in the Products Completed Operations Hazard (PCOH). As a result, the court found that fifth-layer excess insurer American Guarantee and Liability Insurance Companies (AIGLIC) owes no indemnity coverage to NFL, because the first layer insurer, TIG, did not have an aggregate limit and the settlement capped the possible award for any one player below TIG’s per occurrence limit.

The underlying MDL, Matter of National Football League Players’ Concussion Injury Litig., 307 FRD 351, 361 (E.D Pa 2015), aff’d 821 F3d 410 (3d Cir 2016), cert denied 580 US 1030 (2016) consolidated the claims of approximately 5,000 players and over 300 “substantially similar lawsuits.” Discover Prop & Cas., 2026 WL 2948933 at *2. The MDL settlement provides three benefits to players suffering from “qualifying diagnoses” like chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), including an uncapped monetary settlement with caps on individual awards that limited each player with a qualifying diagnosis to a maximum award between $1.5- $5 million, depending on certain variables. Id. at *3.

TIG had two policies that covered the NFL. The first was a primary general liability policy with a $1 million per occurrence limit, and the second was a follow form excess policy covering the next $15 million per occurrence. AIGLIC issued the fifth layer excess liability policy to the NFL that followed form to the TIG primary Policy. TIG, which defended pursuant to a reservation or rights, did not dispute the TIG Policy had no aggregate limit for most claims, but maintained that the losses fell under the Products Completed Operations Hazard (“PCOH”), which had a $1 million aggregate limit. Id. at *4. Thus, there were only two ways the NFL claims could trigger the AIGLIC policy: first, if all of the player’s concussions were considered to be a single occurrence, they could exceed the underlying policy limits. Second, if the claims fell within the PCOH coverage, which had a $1 million aggregate, they could exceed the underlying limits. TIG maintained that the claims constituted a single occurrence and also maintained that they fell within the PCOH coverage so the aggregate limit would be exhausted. AIGLIC argued its policy could not be triggered because each player’s alleged injury constitutes a separate occurrence and because NFL football is not a “product” so the PCOH aggregate limit was not triggered. Id. at 3-4. The court agreed with AIGLIC on all points.

Relevant Policy Language: The TIG Policy’s $1 million PCOH aggregate coverage limit was the “‘most’ TIG would ‘pay’ under Coverage A for damages because of ‘bodily injury’ and ‘property damage’ included in the ‘products-completed operations hazard,” including a “limited category” of bodily injury claims occurring “away from the premises the insured owned or rented which arose from ‘your product’ or ‘your work’ excepts products that are still in the insured’s physical possession or work that has not yet been completed or abandoned.” Id. at *6 (emphasis in original) (cleaned up). Used therein, “your product” meant “‘goods or products, other than real property, manufactured, sold, handled, distributed or disposed of’ by the insured, others trading under the insured’s name, and ‘containers (other than vehicles), materials, parts or equipment furnished in connection with such goods or products.” Id. (cleaned up).

The TIG Policy was also endorsed with “Liability to Participants” coverage – Coverage D – pursuant to which TIG agreed to “pay those sums that the Insured becomes legally obligated to pay as damages because of ‘bodily injury to any ‘participant’ subject to the limits of insurance.” Id. “Participants” included players. Id. The AIGLIC Policy provided the same coverage for damages covered by the TIG Policy.

The Appellate Division deemed the question of the number of occurrences to be the threshold inquiry. TIG argued that all of the players’ injuries were due to the singular event of NFL football, regardless of the time, place, manner or number of hits sustained in their career. Thus, according to TIG, the injuries arose from on common event that was “part of the same causal continuum, without intervening agents or factors.” Id., at *8. The court rejected this argument. Applying New York’s “unfortunate events test”, the court found that each player’s individual injuries constituted a single occurrence. Id. The court first looked at the TIG Policy’s “occurrence” definition “for the suggestion of an intent to group claims” then consider “whether there is a close temporal and spatial relationship between the incidents giving rise to injury or loss, and whether the incidents can be viewed as part of the same causal continuum without intervening agents or factors.” Id. TIG conceded there was no grouping language in its policy but posited that that an “ongoing single-occurrence finding is warranted under the ‘unfortunate event test’” because all players with Qualifying Diagnoses sustained those diagnoses the same way – “playing the singular event of NFL football.” Id. The court disagreed because the incident giving rise to the players’ injuries was not playing NFL football, but rather the head impacts, which took place at different times, on different fields, over at least two decades. Id. Those impacts, which affected thousands of former players who played thousands of games over decades in 90 different stadiums lacked the “temporal and spatial characteristics” required to unify them as a single occurrence, which the court concluded could not be said to have been “precipitated by a single causal continuum.” Id.

The court also rejected the position that the TIG Policy’s “occurrence” definition – “all bodily injury and property damage arising out of continuous or repeated exposure to substantially the same general conditions shall be considered as arising out of one occurrence” – meant all players injuries should be considered a single occurrence. Without aggregation-of-claims language identifying “repeated head impacts” as the operative incident that would give rise to liability, and nothing suggesting the head impacts constituted exposure to the same generally harmful conditions, the court was constrained to find grouping was not appropriate under the policy language and applied the results of the “unfortunate events test” to find at least one occurrence per player. Id. at **9-10.

The court also overturned the Supreme Court’s finding that NFL football was a “product” under the PCOH coverage. The lower court had concluded the term “product” could, as a matter of “common speech” include intangible items like NFL football. The Appellate Division found this reading failed to comport with the purpose of products-hazard coverage, which is meant to insure the party responsible for sending goods into the marketplace, protecting the insured from the risk of loss that occurs when the product leaves the seller’s normal business premises and causes damage elsewhere. In looking beyond, the policy language and finding a broader definition for the word “product” the Supreme Court ignored the reasonable expectations of the average insured purchasing PCOH coverage. The Court said it was improper to isolate the word ‘product’ from its context. “The plain language indicates that the product, as expected to be covered by the PCOH, is a tangible/physical product. Supreme Court should not have expanded the definition of ‘product’ to include intangible products simply because that interpretation is possible.” Id. at 12.

With multiple occurrences in play and no ‘product’ to bring the claims within the PCOH coverage, there was no possibility that the MDL settlement payments would ever reach AIGLIC’s $51 million threshold, so AIGLIC owed no coverage.

Discover highlights the uncertainty that can result when the meaning of undefined policy terms become the lynchpin between coverage and no coverage, and the importance of tying policy language to the nature of the risks meant to be insured against, particularly during the current explosion of artificial intelligence offerings, which can straddle the definition of product and service.

In the interest of brevity, we focused on two of the key rulings in this case. See the full opinion for why the court rejected TIG’s positions that: 1) football players neurodegenerative diseases do not constitute an “occurrence” because they are an inherent risk of the intentional violent impacts of NFL play; 2) the NFL could not meet its burden of showing that players recovering under the settlement did not sustain their injuries during the policy periods; 3) NFL’s notice of claim was untimely, and 4) NFL did not suffer a ‘loss’ because it was allegedly indemnified by the NFL Clubs. The court also discussed why the settlement was reasonable.

text:
The Buffalo Bills got a week to heal.

The Baltimore Ravens gave Lamar Jackson another week to do the same.

Jackson missed his third straight game Sunday because of an ankle injury, and Baltimore lost 35-13 to the Cincinnati Bengals without him.

Now the Ravens have to decide whether the extra time was enough to get their quarterback back for Buffalo.

The Bills come out of their Week 7 bye hoping to get wide receiver D.J. Moore and defensive tackle Ed Oliver back after both missed the previous two games.

Baltimore also picked up another injury Sunday when rookie guard Vega Ioane left because of a knee injury.

Buffalo (5-1) hosts Baltimore (4-3) at 1 p.m. ET Sunday, Nov. 1, at Highmark Stadium.

NFL teams have to submit a report on practice participation on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday for a Sunday game. A game status report is due by 4 p.m. Friday for Sunday games.

Here is the Bills vs. Ravens injury update for Week 8:

Buffalo Bills injury update for Week 8

D.J. Moore, WR, shoulder

D.J. Moore has not played since Oct. 4.

Moore missed Buffalo's final two games before the bye after aggravating the injury against the New England Patriots in Week 4.

He did not practice Wednesday or Thursday before the Raiders game but returned on a limited basis Friday and was listed as questionable. Buffalo ultimately kept him inactive.

Moore originally suffered the shoulder injury against the Detroit Lions in Week 2. He returned the following week and played through it before aggravating the injury against New England.

Ed Oliver, DL, knee

Ed Oliver also missed Buffalo's final two games before the bye.

Oliver suffered his knee injury during the Bills' Week 4 loss to New England when former Buffalo fullback Reggie Gilliam hit his left leg near the sideline.

He missed five consecutive practices before returning on a limited basis the Friday before the Raiders game.

Oliver was listed as questionable but inactive in Las Vegas.

Dalton Kincaid, TE, ribs

Dalton Kincaid left Buffalo's victory over Las Vegas because of a rib injury but was able to return.

Kincaid went to the medical tent and then the locker room during the third quarter after appearing uncomfortable following a route.

The Bills listed him as questionable to return. Kincaid came back in the fourth quarter and caught a 14-yard pass three plays later.

Bradley Chubb, OLB, ribs

Bradley Chubb also left the Raiders game in Week 6 because of a rib injury and returned.

Chubb went out during the second quarter and was initially listed as questionable. He returned later in the first half and played 21 of Buffalo's 66 defensive snaps against Las Vegas.

T.J. Sanders, DL, shoulder

T.J. Sanders played against Las Vegas and recorded one tackle after being listed as questionable because of a shoulder injury.

Dee Alford, CB, ankle

Dee Alford returned against Las Vegas in Week 6 after missing Buffalo's win over the Los Angeles Rams in Week 5 because of an ankle injury. He had two tackles and one pass breakup in the victory over the Raiders.

Joshua Palmer, WR, shoulder

Joshua Palmer returned against Las Vegas after missing the Rams game because of a shoulder injury. He caught one pass for 37 yards against the Raiders.

C.J. Gardner-Johnson, S, suspended

C.J. Gardner-Johnson will not play against Baltimore. It's not because of injury.

The NFL suspended Gardner-Johnson without pay for one game after he spit at a Raiders player during the second quarter of Buffalo's Week 6 victory. Gardner-Johnson was ejected in the second quarter.

His suspension begins Oct. 26 and he can return to Buffalo's active roster Nov. 2, meaning he will miss Sunday's game against Baltimore.

Buffalo Bills injured reserve

Zane Durant, DL, neck

Zane Durant is eligible to return after beginning the season on injured reserve.

Buffalo can designate Durant to return and open his 21-day practice window when he is medically cleared.

Buffalo Bills physically unable to perform

Tyrell Shavers, WR, knee

Tyrell Shavers is eligible to return after beginning the season on the physically unable to perform list.

Shavers is recovering from the torn ACL he suffered during Buffalo's wild-card playoff victory last season.

The Bills can designate him to return and open his 21-day practice window when he is ready.

Buffalo Bills non-football injury

Dorian Strong, CB, neck

Baltimore Ravens injury update for Week 8

Lamar Jackson, QB, ankle

Lamar Jackson will be the biggest injury to monitor this week.

Jackson has missed Baltimore's last three games because of an ankle injury suffered Oct. 4.

He returned to practice last week and was limited Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. Jackson told reporters Friday that the ankle was improving but that running remained the issue.

"I'm just trying to move how I move," Jackson said. "If I can't do that, I can't help my team."

Baltimore listed Jackson as questionable against the Cincinnati Bengals before ruling him out Saturday. Tyler Huntley started for the third consecutive game and threw for 215 yards in the first half of Sunday's loss.

The Ravens are 1-2 without Jackson.

text:
Monday morning brought injury updates on Green Bay Packers center Sean Rhyan, who left Sunday's loss to the Detroit Lions in the first quarter, and starting linebacker Zaire Franklin, who didn't play Sunday after injuring his shin in practice on Thursday.

According to Ian Rapoport of NFL Network, Rhyan is believed to have suffered a high-ankle sprain when Josh Jacobs fell into the back of his legs to finish off a run on the Packers' first drive. While more testing will be done on Monday, this type of ankle injury typically comes with a 4–6-week recovery timeline, so Rhyan will miss Thursday night against the Carolina Panthers and is a candidate for injured reserve.

Jacob Monk is the backup center, but he suffered a quad injury after replacing Rhyan in the first quarter and didn't return. Coach Matt LaFleur didn't think Rhyan or Monk would be available to go against the Panthers. John Williams played the final 58 snaps at center and could start on Thursday night. Rookie Jager Burton is another option, but he was inactive on Sunday.

The Packers won't have their starting center and probably won't have Franklin, one of their defensive captains, against the Panthers. Per Rapoport, Franklin has a hairline fracture in his leg after getting accidently kicked in the shin during Thursday's practice. Expecting him to be physically ready to play in a game just a week after this injury is probably unreasonable. The Packers have not placed Franklin on injured reserve, so it's possible he'll return within the four-week window. But Jonathan Gannon's defense will likely need Isaiah McDuffie and Ty'Ron Hopper to play all the snaps at linebacker against the Panthers.

More injury updates are likely to come later on Monday. LaFleur will answer questions from the media, and the Packers will release their first injury report of Week 8.

NFL Week 7 injury roundup: Christian McCaffrey, Jaylen Waddle and more appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The 2026 NFL season has already been filled with plenty of surprises. But as the midpoint of the season draws closer, some of the funkiness of the early season is beginning to even out. Only one NFL team remains undefeated and another winless following Week 7.

Sunday's games did not include headline-grabbing injuries like the past couple of weeks. However, NFL fans should keep an eye on all of these situations as the league's playoff picture will soon start coming into focus.

There are the most important injuries to watch following an exciting Week 7 of NFL action.

Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)

Christian McCaffrey, San Francisco 49ers

The 49ers have dealt with so many injuries already this season. So when McCaffrey went down, 49ers fans probably started fearing the worst. Fortunately, McCaffrey's injury does not look too serious.

McCaffrey suffered a thigh injury during the first quarter against the Falcons. He left the game briefly, but was able to return in the second half.

CMC explained that his leg "just died on me" and it was difficult to get back on track throughout the rest of the game. Still, McCaffrey declared that he doesn't expect the injury to bother him moving forward.

San Francisco is now on its bye week, so McCaffrey will have extra time to get back to 100%.

Jaylen Waddle, Denver Broncos

The Broncos got cute and it ended up hurting them badly.

Denver dialed up a tricky reverse pitch play for Waddle with just under five minutes left in Sunday's win over Arizona. There was a fumble on the play and Waddle jumped on the ball to prevent a turnover.

Unfortunately, Waddle suffered a chest injury on the play and did not return to the game. Sean Payton took the blame for the awful play call immediately after the victory.

It remains to be seen how severe Waddle's injury really is. Broncos fans should keep their eyes peeled for an injury update on Waddle before Week 8.

Olaivavega Ioane, Baltimore Ravens

The Ravens lost Ioane to a knee injury during Sunday's loss to the Bengals. He did not return to finish the game.

The entire second half was a disaster for Baltimore, as they surrendered 35 unanswered points to Cincinnati in a tough divisional loss. Ioane's injury makes that result even worse.

Ravens fans should keep their eyes on the injury report ahead of Week 8 against the Bills. That could provide clues on the status of QB Lamar Jackson, too.

Taylor Moton, Carolina Panthers

Injuries just keep coming for the Panthers.

Not only did Carolina get absolutely destroyed by Tampa Bay, they also lost yet another offensive tackle. Moton fractured his fibula in Sunday's loss and will be out "a while" per head coach Dave Canales.

The Panthers are already without Ikem Ekwonu and Stone Forsythe at the position. That leaves Rasheed Walker and rookie Monroe Freeling as starters with practically no depth behind them.

Carolina's lack of health on the o-line could be a problem moving forward.

Sean Rhyan, Green Bay Packers

Green Bay suffered even more offensive line injuries in Week 7 against Detroit.

Packers center Sean Rhyan suffered an ankle injury early in Sunday's game and did not return. NFL insider Ian Rapoport reported on Monday that Rhyan's injury is believed to be a high ankle sprain.

"X-Rays were negative, and he has an MRI today. But high-ankle sprains are often 4-6 week injuries," Rapoport added.

Meanwhile, the Packers lost even more depth after Jacob Monk left the game with a quad injury.

Perhaps Green Bay will need to add even more veteran depth on the o-line after a truly disastrous first half of the season.

Cam Skattebo, New York Giants

Skattebo is officially out of the dog house.

The young running back ripped off 17 carries for 124 rushing yards and a touchdown against a tough Texans defense. But Skattebo appeared to injure himself on his biggest play of the game.

Skattebo reportedly felt something in his hamstring during his 42-yard overtime run that set up Devin Singletary for the walk-off touchdown.

Fortunately, NFL insider Mike Garafolo reported on Monday that "all indications this morning are he should be OK." The Giants are on their bye in Week 8, so Skattebo will have some extra rehab time as well.

In other Giants injury news, Tyrone Tracy Jr. left Sunday's game with a hamstring injury and did not return.

Rashid Shaheed, Seattle Seahawks

The Seahawks got a huge win against the Chiefs on Sunday Night Football. But it came at the cost of losing multiple players to injuries.

Shaheed collided with his teammate Jaxon Smith-Njigba in the end zone towards the end of the first half. He apparently suffered a knee injury and did not return for the second half. Shaheed plays a big role on offense and special teams for Seattle, so losing him for a long stretch would be a tough blow. Hopefully Seattle gives an update on his status on Monday.

In other Seahawks injury news, Charles Cross (ankle) and Velus Jones Jr. (hamstring) also left Sunday's game and did not return.

Aaron Jones, Minnesota Vikings

The Vikings just keep shuffling running backs this season.

Jordan Mason finally returned to action on Sunday following his thumb injury. He returned just in time to take over for Jones, who held down the fort while Mason was injured.

Jones left Sunday's game with a knee injury after ripping off a 17-yard run. He did not return.

ESPN's Kevin Seifert explained that Jones was already playing with a sprained left MCL before that injury. Hopefully Jones did not reaggravate that injury. It would be a shame if Minnesota lost their star running back after their undefeated start to the season.

Other notable injuries from Week 7 include Jets DT T'Vondre Sweat (knee), Saints safety Justin Reid (concussion), Texans WR Jaylin Noel (turf toe), and Lions CB Ennis Rakestraw Jr. (ankle).

title: NFL Week 7 Lessons: Don't Be Fooled by the Steelers' Three-Game Winning Streak
description:
It’s still not time to believe in the Steelers I’ve been burned by the Steelers’ vortex of mediocrity a handful of times.
Don’t be fooled by Pittsburgh’s three-game winning streak, including Sunday’s victory over New Orleans.
That shouldn’t be enough to believe this will be the year the Steelers (5–2) end their seven-game playoff losing streak.
The Steelers won a 30–27 shootout against the Bengals in Week 3, then lost 27–24 to the Browns.
Perhaps Sheppard figured out what was wrong with his defense over the bye week because the unit looked different on Sunday.
text:
A few illusions might have developed from Sunday’s games.

The 49ers are no longer undefeated after losing 29–20 to the Falcons. Was this just a trap game, or is this the start of trouble for the injury-ravaged 49ers? It might be difficult to trust this team as a Super Bowl contender moving forward.

The Steelers are on a three-game winning streak after defeating the Saints, 16–10, in Paris, but it may be wise to hold off on saying this will be the year they’ll go far in the postseason. Should Pittsburgh get credit for beating up on three two-win teams?

Then there are the Rams, who got by the Raiders, 35–21. It was an impressive rushing performance, but was this a get-right game or just a one-week anomaly in Las Vegas?

Let’s break down a few of these potential illusions from the Week 7 schedule.

It’s still not time to believe in the Steelers

I’ve been burned by the Steelers’ vortex of mediocrity a handful of times. It’s a cycle that can look appealing at times, but it ended the same way for nearly a decade.

Don’t be fooled by Pittsburgh’s three-game winning streak, including Sunday’s victory over New Orleans. That shouldn’t be enough to believe this will be the year the Steelers (5–2) end their seven-game playoff losing streak.

Yes, there’s plenty to like about Pittsburgh’s positive stretch. The defense has been outstanding the past two weeks, and that unit was enough to overcome an up-and-down outing from Aaron Rodgers and his offense in the win over the Saints. (The Steelers only generated one touchdown and averaged 5.4 yards per gain.) Rodgers was better in the wins against the Colts and Buccaneers, but that’s three victories against a trio of teams that have two wins apiece.

It’s still tough to see the Steelers having enough firepower to hang with the AFC’s best in January. Pittsburgh prefers to slow down games because it has to with a 42-year-old Rodgers who occasionally has trouble getting the ball downfield to DK Metcalf (only two catches for 56 yards on Sunday). But they’re a well-balanced operation with underrated running back Jaylen Warren (18 carries, 101 yards). Additionally, the defense has turned a corner since the back-to-back rocky performances against divisional foes Cincinnati and Cleveland. The Steelers won a 30–27 shootout against the Bengals in Week 3, then lost 27–24 to the Browns.

If the game script goes their way, the Steelers are a tough out against most teams. However, the script hasn’t gone their way when it matters most, as evidenced by six one-and-done playoff appearances.

Pittsburgh has Cleveland and Cincinnati coming up again for its next two games. Perhaps I’ll start falling for the Steelers again if Rodgers outpaces Joe Burrow a second time and the defense shuts down the pesky Browns after the Week 4 loss during Thursday Night Football.

But for now, the Steelers’ three-game winning streak is misleading because they’ve faced three losing teams. Don’t trust them just yet.

49ers’ injury crisis continues to put damper on strong first half

It’s hard to get excited about what the 49ers have done during the first half of the season.

On one hand, they’re 6–1 with a sizable lead in the NFC West standings. On the other hand, the injuries haven’t stopped, and they finally lost a game, falling to the Falcons on Sunday.

It’s probably best to look at the full sample size here to not let one bad game in Atlanta diminish everything San Francisco has done for nearly two months. This is the best team in football, but this is also a team you can’t trust because of the injury waves.

Here’s a scenario we might be headed toward: the top-seeded 49ers being viewed as an underdog in a home playoff game because of several injuries to key players.

Heading into the Falcons game, concerns arose that the 49ers might not have enough healthy players to fill up the 48 game-day roster spots. They were without Mike Evans, Nick Bosa and Deebo Samuel Sr., and that doesn’t include the many players on injured reserve. On Sunday, San Francisco played for a stretch without Christian McCaffrey, who sustained a thigh injury.

I’ve already gone back and forth on my early assessment that the 49ers possibly not being true Super Bowl contenders because of all the injuries. Maybe this season has a ceiling, like last year, when this injury-ravaged team gassed out against the Seahawks in the divisional round.

For now, I’ll trust that the 49ers will get healthy at the right time, but that’s not a given with all the injury waves the past few seasons. San Francisco could afford to miss a few key players, but it needs Evans and McCaffrey to be true contenders in January.

Rams’ simplistic formula leads to bounce-back win in Las Vegas

Injuries forcing the Rams to simplify their operation could be a turning point in their season.

Coach Sean McVay called several running plays and ran the passing attack through Puka Nacua during a much-needed win over the Raiders. The Rams didn’t use flashy three-tight-end formations or forced plays to keep players involved.

The Rams (3–4) were physical and kept it simple, running the ball 38 times for a season-high 199 rushing yards against the Raiders. It was the first time since Week 1 that Matthew Stafford (23-of-29, 195 yards, 3 TDs, INT) didn’t record at least 30 passes, and the season opener doesn’t really count because Stafford didn’t finish the blowout loss against the 49ers. Stafford has already thrown over 50 passes in three games already this season.

The heavy passing attack is partly why Los Angeles only had two victories after six games. The Rams dug themselves a sizable hole in the standings without an identity on the field or a real voice to guide them through adversity, despite having a whopping 11 captains. It was as if McVay didn’t want to hurt anyone’s feelings and prioritized getting everyone involved.

But wide receiver Davante Adams, edge rusher Myles Garrett, tight end Terrance Ferguson and defensive tackles Poona Ford and Kobie Turner weren’t available for Sunday’s game in Las Vegas. The Rams also nearly didn’t have Nacua after he sustained a calf injury in practice earlier this week.

The Rams have plenty of talent, but they’re hard to beat with Nacua as the focal point of a well-balanced offense. McVay might also have finally found the formula for getting the most from his two running backs, Kyren Williams (16 carries, 99 yards, TD) and Blake Corum (17 carries, 93 yards, TD), the duo that combined for 192 rushing yards in Las Vegas.

If McVay continues to commit to the run, Williams and Corum will likely deliver more performances like that. This team might be close to finally forming an identity.

Lions’ defense finally shows improvements

It’s not surprising that the Lions defeated the Packers, 20–17. But few expected Detroit’s defense to stifle an offense that had been rolling for a few weeks and recently got back running back Josh Jacobs.

It was the kind of performance defensive coordinator Kelvin Sheppard had needed for a long time. It would have been difficult for coach Dan Campbell to continue defending him as his coordinator had Jordan Love lit up this suspect secondary. But Love (27-of-45, 274 yards, two TDs, INT) struggled to connect with emerging second-year wideout Matthew Golden (12 targets, six catches, 39 yards) and probably should have been picked off two or three times if Lions’ defenders hadn’t dropped balls.

Detroit (4–2) held Green Bay (4–3) to 324 yards and only 17 first downs. Perhaps Sheppard figured out what was wrong with his defense over the bye week because the unit looked different on Sunday. It also certainly helped that the team got back versatile safety Brian Branch, who registered an interception in his season debut.

Having a reliable defense would go a long way toward bolstering the Lions’ hopes of winning a competitive NFC North. Minnesota leads the division at 6–0, while Chicago sits in second at 5–2.

The Denver Broncos secured their first two-score win of the season on Sunday with a 30-16 victory over the Arizona Cardinals, but the win did come at a cost.

Broncos wide receiver Jaylen Waddle (chest) and defensive lineman Zach Allen (appeared to be hamstring) both went down with injuries in the fourth quarter. Waddle initially stayed down on the field before walking to the sideline and then into the locker room. He was previously limited in two days of practice last week with a chest injury. Denver announced Waddle as questionable to return, but he did not return to Sunday's game after totaling four catches for 48 yards prior to the injury.

Allen also went down in the fourth quarter and appeared to be favoring his right hamstring. After a visit to the team's blue medical tent, Allen was spotted standing on the sideline without his helmet for the end of the game. Allen went to the podium for a post-game press conference after the win and said, "Yeah, I'll be fine. Yeah, I'll be good," when asked about his injury.

Elsewhere on the injury front, cornerback Pat Surtain (ankle) missed his third straight game on Sunday and safety Talanoa Hufanga (ankle) sat out his second consecutive game. After the win, Surtain said, "Not really," when asked by the Denver Gazette's Chris Tomasson if he was close to playing in Arizona. When asked if he'll play against the Chiefs on Sunday, Surtain said, "Possibly." Denver's first injury report of the week will come out on Wednesday.

text:
Green Bay Packers linebacker Zaire Franklin is dealing with a hairline fracture in his leg, while center Sean Rhyan is believed to have suffered a high ankle sprain, sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

Rhyan left Sunday's loss to the Detroit Lions with an ankle injury. X-rays were negative, but he is expected to get an MRI on Monday. Rhyan would be expected to miss four to six weeks if imaging shows a high ankle sprain.

Not only did the Packers lose Rhyan after just four snaps against the Lions, but they also lost primary backup center Jacob Monk to a quad injury after five snaps. Second-year pro John Williams finished the game, playing the final 58 snaps of the game. Those were the first career regular-season snaps Williams has played on offense.

Coach Matt LaFleur said after the game he did not expect Rhyan or Monk to be available for Thursday's game against the Carolina Panthers.

Franklin suffered what LaFleur called a shin injury during a collision in practice last Thursday. On Friday, LaFleur said Franklin is not expected to go on injured reserve, meaning the team believes he will miss fewer than four games.

Although it's Franklin's first year with the Packers after coming to Green Bay in an offseason trade with the Indianapolis Colts, the ninth-year veteran quickly became a key part of the defense. He was elected defensive captain, rare for someone in the first year with a team, and has been the signal-caller for the defense.

Franklin ranks third on the team in tackles (41) and has two quarterback hits, a forced fumble and a pass breakup.

text:
The Detroit Lions secured a massive divisional win over the Green Bay Packers on Sunday.

Playing their first divisional opponent of the season, the Lions overcame some mistakes and were ultimately able to earn a hard-fought 20-17 victory over the Packers to advance to 4-2 on the season.

Running back Jahmyr Gibbs played a pivotal part in the victory, notchng 116 rushing yards on 29 carries. The dynamic running back played a key part on the final drive, as he converted the final third-down to cement the win.

On that game-sealing run, however, Gibbs landed awkwardly trying to slide onto the turf inbounds to keep the clock running and prevent the Packers from getting the ball back. Though the landing wasn't smooth, head coach Dan Campbell stated that he should be okay during his postgame press conference.

"We got him checked. He should be good. That's that whole, is it really worth going down?" Campbell said. "Or should he just go score? Sometimes I question that. Maybe he should've just (scored). But, all good. That's a good win."

Gibbs had slid to the turf two plays prior, on first-down, two yards short of the chains. This was done in an effort to maintain the running clock, but it nearly backfired after the Lions jumped resulting in a five-yard penalty.

However, on third-and-6, quarterback Jared Goff pitched the ball to Gibbs who burst around the left side before sliding after getting the first down. This allowed the Lions to run the clock all the way down to one second before taking a timeout to set up Jake Bates' game-winning field goal.

Campbell's update is a sigh of relief for Detroit, as Gibbs is one of the team's most dynamic talents and one of the league's best running backs. Signed to a three-year contract extension in the offseason, the Alabama product is off to another strong start through six games in 2026.

Detroit's offseason saw the team deal David Montgomery, who was Gibbs' counterpart in the backfield, to the Houston Texans and cement Gibbs as their top running back moving forward. This has come with an increased workload for him, as he has had at least 20 touches in five of the team's six games.

Up to this point, Gibbs has notched 620 rushing yards and nine total touchdowns, with seven on the ground and two as a receiver. Sunday's game against the Packers marked the first one this year where Gibbs was kept out of the end-zone.

text:
When an NFL player goes down with an injury, the questions come quickly.

What happened? How serious is it? And, perhaps most importantly, how long will he be out?

But according to Denver Broncos team physician and orthopedic surgeon Dr. Aaron Mates, the answers aren’t always as straightforward as fans and analysts might suggest.

Mates, who has worked with professional athletes across the NFL, MLB, NHL and other sports, said the evaluation process involves multiple medical professionals, diagnostic testing and a gradual determination of when an athlete can safely return to activity.

And one of the biggest misconceptions, he said, is that medical clearance automatically means a player is ready to go back out and compete.

“It’s when you say, ‘OK, from a medical standpoint, this player, this patient is fit to progress back toward activity,’” Mates said. “So it doesn’t mean you play tomorrow night.”

Instead, clearance marks the beginning of a progression that can take an athlete from rehabilitation to conditioning, practice and eventually a return to competition.

Inside the injury process

When a player gets injured during an NFL game, Mates described the initial evaluation area on the sideline as a triage tent, similar to an emergency room.

Medical personnel first assess the injury and determine whether the player can safely return or needs additional evaluation.

If further examination is necessary, the player may be taken to the training room for X-rays, additional testing and a more thorough assessment. Depending on the injury, the process can continue after the game with further examinations and imaging to determine the appropriate treatment.

The evaluation involves the head team physician, specialists such as Mates, athletic trainers and the player.

While the medical staff determines whether a return is safe, Mates emphasized that the athlete remains central to the decision-making process.

“Their voice is everything, because they’re the patient,” he said. “It’s no different than being in my clinic, it’s a doctor-patient relationship.”

Physicians must ensure players understand their injuries and treatment options, but they also have the responsibility to prevent an athlete from returning when doing so would be unsafe.

“We can say, ‘You can’t play,’” Mates said. “We can say, ‘This is not safe. We’re not clearing you.’”

That responsibility can become especially complicated when an injury occurs during the season, when teams are competing for a playoff spot or trying to make a postseason run.

Mates said the challenge of sports medicine isn’t necessarily the orthopedic treatment itself, but determining how the timing of an injury affects its management.

With professional athletes facing a limited competitive window, physicians sometimes must consider treatment options more quickly than they might in other circumstances.

“We can’t sit around and wait for something to heal for three months and it doesn’t heal, then do surgery,” he said.

The road back

For athletes recovering from surgery or an injury, Mates described a three-phase process designed to gradually prepare them for competition.

The first phase focuses on rehabilitation and recovery, including physical therapy and regaining strength and mobility.

The second phase shifts toward general conditioning, with activities such as running, jumping, balance work and changes in direction.

The third phase involves returning to the sport itself, including practice, sport-specific drills and simulated game situations.

For example, Mates mentioned he has treated hockey players who must complete land-based drills involving cutting, running and turning before he allows them to put on skates.

Football players follow a similar progression, working with trainers and conditioning staff before advancing toward full practice and game participation.

The goal is to ensure athletes can handle the demands of their sport rather than simply demonstrate that an injury has improved in a controlled medical setting.

The limits of injury reports

Another challenge for doctors comes from the speculation that often follows an injury.

Mates noted he has watched television coverage of athletes he has treated and heard injury assessments that were inaccurate, particularly when commentators attempt to identify an injury from video footage and predict a recovery timeline.

“I can’t tell you how many times I’ve been involved with an athlete who’s been injured, and then flip on whatever, ESPN or whatever, ‘SportsCenter,’ OutKick or whatever, and what they’re saying is completely wrong,” Mates said. “Or they’ll have a so-called specialist talking about what the guy saw on the video during the play, and what that injury is and what the recovery is and all these kind of things, and they’re completely wrong.”

He added that the public generally receives only the information a player and team choose to release because physicians must adhere to HIPAA rules.

That can leave fans with unanswered questions, especially when an injury report uses broad designations such as “day-to-day,” “week-to-week” or “questionable.”

Those labels don’t necessarily provide enough information to determine the severity of an injury or how close a player is to returning.

The uncertainty can become even more pronounced as sports betting increases interest in player availability and injury updates from the moment they happen.

For Mates, the distinction between public speculation and an actual medical evaluation is important: A diagnosis and recovery estimate require more information than what viewers can see during a play.

Advances in sports medicine

Despite concerns about injuries across professional sports, Mates said determining whether injuries are becoming more common requires looking beyond individual cases.

Researchers track injury data across leagues, helping inform safety protocols and rule changes. At the same time, modern athletes are faster and more athletic, potentially changing the physical demands placed on their bodies.

Mates noted advances in surgical techniques, rehabilitation, conditioning and nutrition have also helped change how athletes recover.

“The way we fix Achilles now is not how we did it 15 years ago,” he said. “There’s biological adjuvants, there’s rehab protocols, there’s constantly literature coming out. ... It’s the same across orthopedics. So if you got your knee replaced in 2026, it’s very different than 2010. Now we’re using robots for alignment and placement, back then it was just kind of manual guides.”

Mates also works with emerging treatments and biologic approaches, including platelet-rich plasma and cartilage repair techniques, as part of a broader effort to advance orthopedic care.

He mentioned experience treating elite athletes can help physicians develop approaches that eventually benefit patients outside professional sports.

Ultimately, Mates said, the priority remains the same regardless of the athlete or level of competition: making sure the patient is safe and healthy.

“We’re doctors, not fans,” he said. “So we need to keep that separation.”

There wasn’t much to celebrate after the Kansas City Chiefs’ 20-3 loss to the Seattle Seahawks, but the injury situation might actually be one of those things.

The team was missing several pieces in Week 7, with Tyquan Thornton, Rashee Rice, Jaylon Moore, and Josh Simmons among the injured starters. Another starter on defense got banged up during the game, but his injury doesn’t appear to be anything serious.

“There’s not really any injuries to mention,” Reid said, before mentioning the lone injury. ” Nick (Bolton) had some spasms in his neck, and he’ll work through that and be OK.”

Bolton played some inspired run defense against the Seahawks on Sunday, leading the team with six solo stops, 11 combined tackles, and a tackle for loss. He was dinged in the third quarter, missing just a single snap. Bolton returned to the game and made a play that forced a Seattle field goal, extending the lead to 13. He was staggered a bit later in the second half, but didn’t leave the game.

The good news is that Bolton doesn’t appear to be at any risk of missing time. He’s been a force on defense this year and remains the team’s green dot and defensive play-caller.

The Chiefs should be healthier when they face the Broncos in Week 8

The Chiefs will look to bounce back against an AFC West rival in Week 8. It won’t be easy as they travel to Mile High Stadium to face the Denver Broncos, but the team should be healthier for this game.

Jaylon Moore will have a chance to clear the NFL’s concussion protocol during practice this week. They need him at right tackle for this one because Joshua Ezeudu struggled in his first start. It won’t be any easier facing Jonathon Cooper and Nik Bonitto next Sunday.

Similarly, the Chiefs’ receivers struggled to create separation in Week 7’s loss to Seattle. Rashee Rice isn’t exactly a burner at wide receiver. However, he’s another trusted target who can help open things up in the passing game for Kansas City. Rice is several weeks removed from the initial hamstring injury. He should realistically be able to return to the practice field in some capacity next Wednesday.

The injury bug is taking another chunk out of the San Francisco 49ers.

In what was the latest issue for the injury-riddled Niners, star running back Christian McCaffrey exited the team's Week 7 contest with a thigh ailment.

He was seen on the sideline and taken inside the medical tent. Broadcast cameras also showed the running back getting his left leg worked on.

McCaffrey missed an extended period of time in the first half, and his return was questionable.

It is just the latest injury issue for the Niners, who came into Week 7 without Mike Evans and plenty of other key pieces across the roster.

With a bye week looming in Week 8, San Francisco chose to be cautious with Evans. It remains to be seen how they will proceed with the star running back, who is the key to the Kyle Shanahan offense.

Here's the latest on McCaffrey.

Christian McCaffrey injury update

McCaffrey returned to the game to start the second half.

He warmed up during halftime and was spotted riding the stationary bike on the sideline prior to the start of the third quarter.

McCaffrey was seen jogging back to the locker room with 6:14 remaining in the first half. He didn't have a noticeable limp, but was listed as questionable to return with a thigh injury, the team announced.

The running back was seen getting his leg worked on by the training staff late in the first quarter against the Falcons in Week 7. In his absence, Kaelon Black handled the workload out of the San Francisco backfield. He burst through the defense for a 30-yard rushing touchdown to extend the Niners lead to begin the second quarter.

Jordan James is next in line behind Black on the depth chart.

"It sucks because I feel like I was going on a run there," McCaffrey said after the game. "My leg just died on me, just tried to get it going for the whole rest of the game. It just sucks having to play like that. I know I'll be alright, but it's just really frustrating."

text:
With six weeks still remaining between now and what could be the final weekend ever of NCAA conference championships, so many schools still have plenty to play for, but one player will be shifting their focus to the 2027 NFL Draft a little earlier than expected. According to ESPN’s Pete Thamel, top offensive tackle prospect Trevor Goosby suffered a knee injury this weekend and will miss the rest of his senior season, as a result.

Originally a three-star offensive tackle recruit out of Melissa HS (TX), Goosby’s first offers came from smaller schools like UT-San Antonio and nearby North Texas. He began getting interest and offers from some Power conference schools like Kansas and Oklahoma State, and near the end of his junior year, Goosby committed to a close-to-home Power 5 option in TCU. Early into the summer, though, the Longhorns came calling and floated him an offer. He scheduled an official visit for two weeks later, and at the end of the three-day courting ritual, he flipped his commitment to Texas.

Goosby had a lot of work to do once he arrived in Austin. He only made two game appearances as a true freshman and only saw garbage-time snaps and special teams work for most of his sophomore campaign, sitting behind future first-round pick Kelvin Banks Jr. Late in the season, though, Banks exited a rivalry game against Texas A&M early with an injury, and Goosby was tapped to fill in,. He would be asked to start at left tackle for the team’s conference championship against Georgia, as well.

In the College Football Playoff, Goosby filled in for another future NFL draft pick in right tackle Cameron Williams after Williams exited the school’s first-round game against Clemson with an injury. He started at right tackle for the Longhorns’ two last playoff games against Arizona State and Ohio State before getting eliminated.

Having proven he could handle work on the first-team offense under the brightest of lights, Goosby opened up his third year in Austin as the starting left tackle, and he’s held the role ever since. He earned first-team All-SEC honors in his first season as a full-time starter, and as the blindside blocker for the player many predicted might be the No. 1 overall pick of the 2027 NFL Draft, Goosby came into the 2026 campaign billed as a likely Day 1 pick himself.

ESPN’s Jordan Reid ranked Goosby as the fourth-best offensive tackle prospect and the 30th-best prospect overall just over a week ago. Pro Football Focus (subscription required) reset their big board three weeks ago, and Goosby checked in as the top overall offensive line prospect and the seventh-best prospect in the class. Listed by the school at 6-foot-7 and 325 pounds, the 21-year-old boasts elite size without sacrificing any athleticism or movement.

Goosby came into the season surrounded by expectations that he would become one of the first offensive lineman taken in the draft. He was sure to have challengers, though, as Texas stumbled recently, losing two games in a row, before returning to the win column this weekend.

Now, both Goosby and his team will have new challenges to confront. The Longhorns will look to stay alive in competition for a spot in the 12-team College Football Playoff, and Goosby will need to work his way back to full health. The injury will almost certainly impact his draft stock, and he could always choose to return to school if it damages his prospects too much. Until a clearer picture and timeline are produced, though, it’s difficult to determine how severe the impact will be.

text:
A week after suffering a concussion, Cleveland Browns safety Grant Delpit needed help leaving the field again Sunday against the Tennessee Titans.

Delpit took a blow to the head from teammate Adin Huntington and walked off with trainers while appearing to favor his neck. He initially looked to stay in the game but an official called trainers over, stopping the play. The collision left Cleveland with another injury concern involving one of its most important defenders.

The nature and severity of Delpit's injury were not immediately clear. A second concussion had not been confirmed.

UPDATE: Delpit did return to the game in the fourth quarter, avoiding concussion protocol.

Delpit had only just been cleared to return. He suffered a concussion during the Browns' October 18 win over the Baltimore Ravens and was ruled out after leaving in the first quarter. Cleveland announced Saturday that he had cleared the NFL's concussion protocol, removing his injury designation for the trip to Tennessee.

He had missed Wednesday's practice before participating on a limited basis Thursday and Friday. The Browns' final injury report listed both a concussion and a shoulder issue.

Browns Defense Responds After Another Slow Start

The injury interrupted another uneven afternoon for a Cleveland defense that has repeatedly recovered from rough starts.

Tony Pollard scored on Tennessee's first two possessions, putting the Browns in a 14-0 hole with 8:35 remaining in the first quarter.

The response was considerably better. The Browns delivered a goal-line stand after replay overturned another apparent Pollard touchdown, keeping Tennessee from extending its lead to 21-7.

Denzel Ward then intercepted Cam Ward in the second quarter, recording the 20th interception of his career and his second this season. Those stops helped Cleveland recover and take a 17-14 lead into halftime.

The pattern was familiar. Against Baltimore, the Browns allowed 10 points on the Ravens' first two possessions before shutting them out the rest of the way in a 13-10 victory.

"Early on, after 10 points, shutting them out and constantly getting us the ball back and giving us a chance to win," head coach Todd Monken said.

Mason Graham Returns After Brief Injury Scare

The Browns also had a scare involving Mason Graham, who briefly hobbled off the field before returning to the game. Sunday marked the defensive tackle's first appearance since he suffered knee and ankle injuries against the Pittsburgh Steelers on October 1. Graham missed the games against the New York Jets and Ravens before returning against Tennessee.

Graham sustained a left MCL sprain and an ankle sprain. He was limited in practice Wednesday and Thursday before participating fully Friday.

Graham's return restored one of Cleveland's most productive pass rushers. The second-year tackle recorded four sacks in the first three games and still led the team entering Week 7 despite missing two contests. Cleveland entered Sunday with 19 sacks, with 11 players contributing at least one.

With fellow defensive tackle Mike Hall Jr. out for a third consecutive game with an ankle injury, keeping Graham available became even more important.

In a game the Falcons desperately needed to win, Daniels came through with a team-high 11 tackles, made a crucial interception in the fourth quarter and, for good measure, recovered a fumble that finished off a 29-20 win over the previously unbeaten San Francisco 49ers.

“I'm really proud of that kid,” said coach Kevin Stefanski, who rewarded the 23-year-old linebacker with a game ball.

Once he left the hospital and was cleared physically, Daniels faced the inevitable mental challenge of getting back on the field without any lingering doubts or fears holding him back. He knew that his facemask-on-knee collision with Chicago Bears tight end Colston Loveland could have turned out much worse.

“I've never not walked off the field after an injury,” Daniels said. “So mentally, I had to be prepared. Going back home, I had to make sure I was OK mentally, more than anything, and not playing timid.”

No one would accuse him of timidity against Brock Purdy and the Niners.

Daniels turned up everywhere, making the sort of big plays the Falcons (3-4) needed to pick up their first home win of the season. Especially in the final quarter, when the fourth-round draft pick looked like a budding star with Atlanta clinging to a 26-20 lead.

On third-and-9 from just shy of midfield, Purdy attempted a pass over the middle. Daniels read it all the way, leaping high to deflect the ball into his own hands. With the pick secured, he took off the other way for a 29-yard return that set up Nick Folk's field goal with 1:56 remaining.

“I had missed one earlier in the game,” Daniels said. “I just knew I needed to make a play for my team.”

Daniels wasn't done, either.

The 49ers tried to race down the field for a touchdown or field goal that would've at least given them a shot at an onside kick. But Jessie Bates jarred the ball loose from George Kittle after a long completion, and Daniels, hustling all the way, fell on the fumble at the Falcons 20 with 47 seconds to go.

Bring on the victory formation.

Teammate Maason Smith marveled at how far Daniels had come in the past week.

“I can remember on Monday, he could barely turn his neck to either side,” Smith said. “To see him go through all that, then come back on the following Sunday and have a hell of a game is great to see. I hope to see more of it.”

Daniels conceded that he was still thinking about the injury when he came out for the warmups at Mercedes-Benz Stadium, a player alone with his thoughts after a harrowing ordeal.

“I wasn’t scared, but I definitely thought about it,” Daniels said. “I haven’t been in full pads all week. What if I’m not OK? But once I got my first tackle in pregame, I was good.”

He wouldn't get any argument from the 49ers, who lost for the first time this season largely because of four turnovers.

The Falcons can only hope their young linebacker's inspiring recovery signals a long-term turnaround for a long-suffering franchise.

Daniels is certainly looking forward. When fellow rookie linebacker Harold Perkins Jr. was slapping him on the back of his helmet in celebration as the final seconds ticked way, leaving the field the previous Sunday on a stretcher was long forgotten.

“That was the last thing I was worried about,” Daniels said with a grin.

Just when the Texas offense got back on track against Ole Miss, it lost one of its best players. Left tackle Trevor Goosby has suffered a season-ending knee injury, multiple outlets report.

Goosby went down during the first quarter of the Longhorns' 34-27 win over the Rebels on Saturday night, and he was carted off the field. After undergoing evaluation in the locker room, Goosby returned to the sideline on crutches.

The loss of Goosby is a massive one for the Horns, a team that has struggled to find consistency on offense. A fourth-year tackle, Goosby is considered one of the top offensive linemen in the country, and he projects as a first-round NFL Draft pick.

Not only does Goosby bring experience to the offensive line with 22 starts over the last three seasons, but he has the talent and accolades to go along with it. Goosby earned All-SEC honors in 2025, and he was a preseason first-team All-American at CBS Sports.

In the immediate aftermath of the Ole Miss game, Sarkisian couldn't provide updates on Goosby or star wide receiver Cam Coleman, both of whom suffered what appeared to be significant injuries.

"Well, I think, I don't have all the particulars on Cam (Coleman) and Trevor (Goosby)," Sarkisian said. "Obviously, neither of them look very good."

Andre Cojoe replaced Goosby at left tackle, and he did an admirable job in relief as Ole Miss sacked Arch Manning just twice. Although Cojoe hasn't played as many games as Goosby, he is a senior who has been in the program since he signed with the Longhorns in 2023.

Cojoe missed the entire 2025 season due to injury, but he has appeared in all seven games this season and 11 total games throughout his career, albeit in a limited capacity.

Texas has allowed 2.71 sacks per game, which is tied for 117th nationally, and it's hard to see that improving with Goosby on the shelf.

The top story line heading into the matchup between the Kansas City Chiefs and Seattle Seahawks this week is perhaps running back Kenneth Walker III’s return to his former home to take on his former team, for which he earned Super Bowl MVP honors in February. But on the Chiefs side, at least, the lack of healthy pass-catchers and the status of tight end Travis Kelce is a close second.

Kelce went down with an ankle injury early in the team’s game last weekend against the Los Angeles Chargers following what appeared to be a hip-drop tackle on the part of Chargers linebacker Daiyan Henley in the opening quarter.

“Daiyan Henley’s tackle on Travis Kelce was a sliding hip drop where his shoulder dinged Kelce’s ankle,” PJ Green of the Kansas City Star wrote on X last Sunday.

However, the NFL’s Office of Gameday Accountability disagreed six days later when handing out fines to players across the league it deemed guilty of on-field misconduct during Week 6. Henley’s name did not appear on the list, which means he the NFL will not punish him for the tackle in question.

The league did, however, fine Chargers rookie offensive guard Alex Harkey a total of $5277 for a late hit he committed against the Chiefs at the beginning of the fourth quarter.

Travis Kelce Carrying no Injury Designation Into Chiefs-Seahawks Matchup

While the NFL’s call not to punish Henley may feel like something of a gut-punch to Chiefs fans hoping for accountability for their rivals, there is good news, too, which creates a silver lining heading into Week 7.

Team doctors taped up Kelce’s ankle, underneath and outside of his cleat, last Sunday and the tight end eventually returned to action. He finished the contest with four catches for 53 yards, as Kansas City went on to win by a score of 22-6 and move to a record of 5-0 on the season.

The Chiefs listed Kelce as a limited participant all week in practice due to his ankle injury. However, he entered the weekend without an injury designation, per the team’s official report, which means Kelce is healthy and will be a full-go in Seattle on Sunday, October 25.

Chiefs Looking to Remain Undefeated, Atop AFC Standings With Win in Seattle

With a road victory against the defending champion Seahawks, Kansas City will move to 6-0 and maintain sole possession of first place in the AFC standings.

The San Francisco 49ers are already 6-0, as they have yet to hit their bye week. The Niners play the Falcons in Atlanta on Sunday before getting a much-needed week off for their extensively injured roster.

text:
ATLANTA -- Rookie linebacker Kendal Daniels had the game-sealing interception to help the Atlanta Falcons beat the previously undefeated San Francisco 49ers 29-20 on Sunday, one week after he was immobilized by medical personnel and rushed to Grady Hospital.

Last Sunday against the Chicago Bears, Daniels laid on the turf for nearly eight minutes after taking a knee to the head before departing the field on a cart. Seven days later, he led the Falcons with nine solo tackles and had a fumble recovery in Atlanta's victory.

"It's been the craziest week of my life," Daniels said. "I've never not walked off the field after an injury. So, mentally, I had to be prepared and going back home and just making sure I was OK mentally more than anything and not playing timid, but I've never not gotten up from an injury. So, being stretched off the field ­-- I won't let it happen again. It was a bad feeling, and I'm blessed to be able to play this week."

Falcons head coach Kevin Stefanski called the whole thing "remarkable."

Daniels didn't end up with any structural damage nor a concussion after getting hurt against the Bears in Week 6. He was actually back in the home locker room after the game, walking around under his own power. Daniels was in pain, though. Falcons defensive tackle Maason Smith said Daniels was so sore when he got back to the team's facility Monday that he couldn't move his neck to either side.

By Wednesday, though, Daniels was able to practice. He was listed as questionable on the injury report, but not only did he start Sunday, he wore the green dot, calling plays for the Falcons' defense. Veteran linebacker Divine Deablo would normally have that role, but he was out with a forearm injury.

"And then, oh, by the way, go play in a game against [49ers coach] Kyle Shanahan and [quarterback] Brock Purdy and put the green dot on and call the defense," Stefanski said. "So that's unbelievable to just do that. And then to make a play at the end, man, really proud of that kid."

Daniels' interception came with 2:42 left in the game and the Falcons ahead 26-20. Atlanta was able to get a Nick Folk field goal on the ensuing possession to go up by two possessions. Daniels also recovered a fumble forced by safety Jessie Bates III with 57 seconds left.

"He's a warrior," Falcons tight end Kyle Pitts said of Daniels. "I definitely told him, I was like, 'Damn, I didn't know he was going to be walking that quick.'"

After the interception, fellow rookie linebacker Harold Perkins Jr. couldn't contain himself celebrating with Daniels, who said he didn't even have a chance to remember his neck injury.

"I wasn't thinking of it," Daniels said with a smile. "'Perk' was slapping me in the back of my head. I couldn't breathe. I think that was the last thing I was worried about was last week."

SICscore.com is tracking the latest NFL Week 7 injuries, player statuses, medical updates and potential return timelines from around the league.

Cam Skattebo, Giants - Hamstring

Skattebo reported feeling something in his hamstring during a career-long 42-yard run in overtime against the Texans, causing him to go down at the Houston 30-yard line. The severity of the injury is unclear, but the Giants' Week 8 bye will provide additional recovery time.

Sean Rhyan, Packers - Left Ankle

Rhyan exited Sunday's game against the Lions with a left ankle injury after Josh Jacobs and Aidan Hutchinson rolled onto his ankle from behind. He is questionable to return and was replaced at center by Jacob Monk.

Jacob Monk, Packers - Quad

Monk exited Sunday's game against the Lions with a quadriceps injury shortly after replacing the injured Sean Rhyan at center. He is questionable to return.

Aaron Jones Sr., Vikings - Left Knee

Jones exited Sunday's game against the Colts with a knee injury and did not return. He previously revealed that he had been playing through a sprained MCL in his left knee.

Taylor Moton, Panthers - Left Ankle

Moton suffered a fractured fibula during Sunday's game against the Buccaneers and is out indefinitely, according to head coach Dave Canales. He was carted off after his left leg appeared to get rolled up on. The diagnosis confirms the fracture concern initially raised by Dr. David Chao (@ProFootballDoc) based on video analysis.

Drake London, Falcons - Concussion Evaluation

London was evaluated for a concussion during Sunday's game against the 49ers but was cleared to return. According to Dr. David Chao, London passed the evaluation and returned to game action.

Christian McCaffrey, 49ers - Thigh

McCaffrey returned in the second half against the Falcons after suffering a thigh injury earlier in the game. He was initially listed as questionable to return but was seen running on the sidelines. Dr. David Chao believes the injury appears more consistent with a contusion than a muscle strain based on video analysis.

Tyrone Tracy Jr., Giants - Left Hamstring

Tracy exited Sunday's game against the Texans with a left hamstring injury and did not return. He was seen on the sideline favoring his left leg while attempting to loosen up the hamstring. The Giants have not announced an official diagnosis.

text:
The Baltimore Ravens were forced to make another change along their offensive line Sunday after rookie right guard Vega Ioane suffered a knee injury against the Cincinnati Bengals. Baltimore announced that Ioane was questionable to return. Emery Jones Jr. replaced the rookie first-round pick at right guard, continuing a season of constant movement along the Ravens' offensive front.

Ioane's injury came during his first game back at his natural position. He had started the previous three games at center after injuries depleted Baltimore's depth at the position. Cam Jurgens' return allowed Ioane to move back to right guard against Cincinnati, giving the Ravens their preferred alignment for the first time since acquiring Jurgens from the Philadelphia Eagles.

Jurgens made his Ravens debut at center after clearing the NFL's concussion protocol. He missed Baltimore's previous two games after the trade but practiced fully all week and entered Sunday without an injury designation.

The Ravens were already without guard Andrew Vorhees, who was inactive because of a foot injury. That left Jones as the direct replacement for Ioane. The rookie had previously played right guard when Ioane was forced to move inside.

Baltimore will closely monitor Ioane's availability because its offensive line has already absorbed injuries at nearly every interior position. The Ravens entered the game with three centers on injured reserve and had hoped Jurgens' debut would finally provide stability.

Instead, Ioane's knee injury forced Baltimore to adjust again during an important AFC North matchup. His potential absence would leave Jones responsible for protecting Tyler Huntley and creating running lanes for Derrick Henry against Cincinnati's defensive front.
